bull_thesis: SoftwareOne is a capital-light global reseller and advisor for software and cloud services that, after its July 2025 merger with Crayon, generates roughly CHF 228 million of trailing free cash flow (the cash left after running the business and buying equipment) yet trades at only about seven to eight times that cash — an 11% free-cash-flow yield — with a clean balance sheet holding roughly CHF 345-360 million of net cash (about CHF 1.6 per share). The bull case is a self-funded compounding story. First, the numbers the market can touch are cheap: on enterprise value (market value plus debt, minus cash) the business changes hands at about 1.2 times sales and roughly six to eight times cash flow, versus reseller peers Insight, Computacenter, Bechtle and CDW that trade in the low-to-mid teens on cash flow. Second, the merger is delivering: cost synergies (savings from combining the two firms) are running at CHF 86 million against an CHF 80-100 million target, ahead of plan, and management held the adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, stripped of one-offs) above 20.9% in 2025 while guiding above 23% for 2026 and toward 28% by 2030. Third, the business returned to growth — like-for-like revenue rose 1.4% for 2025 and accelerated to 11% in the fourth quarter, with the North America unit (down 12.6% in 2025) turning up and new wins like becoming Google Cloud's first global authorized distributor. Fourth, generative AI reads as near-term demand, not just threat: management notes 'our business model really thrives around complexity,' and more AI vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI) means more advisory need. Finally, there is dormant optionality — the founders own roughly 29%, once tried to sell the company to private equity at around CHF 18.80 per share, and private-equity take-privates of European software are active again in 2026, so a renewed approach is not off the table. If synergies land and margins march toward the 2030 target, the stock re-rates toward its peer cash-flow multiple, worth roughly CHF 13-14 a share; a take-out would be worth more.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is cheap for reasons, and the reasons are getting harder, not easier. First, the accounting profit is essentially zero — net income of just CHF 0.9 million in 2025 and earnings per share collapsed from CHF 0.76 in 2021 to CHF 0.006, a decline of about 70% a year — so the entire value case rests on trusting management's 'adjusted' add-backs and a lumpy cash-flow figure over the GAAP profit-and-loss. Earnings quality screens weak (a Piotroski score of 3 of 9), and the company beat 0 of its last 7 quarterly consensus prints. Second, the moat is a channel position whose economics are partly set by its biggest supplier: Microsoft's enterprise-agreement rebate changes drove the 12.6% North America revenue decline, and that lever can move against the company again despite management's assurance of 'stabilization' in 2026. Third, the gross margin is contracting (44.1%, about 0.74 standard deviations below its historical peak) as the mix shifts toward lower-value resale — a slow squeeze on the share of the dollar the company keeps. Fourth, the longer-horizon secular risk is real: generative AI is most likely to automate exactly the licensing-optimization and advisory work that is part of SoftwareOne's value-add, and hyperscalers can go direct and re-cut partner economics. Fifth, and most important for timing, the special situation that made this name interesting is over — the Bain/Apax/CVC take-private saga resolved into the Crayon merger, Bain walked, the June 2026 Capital Markets Day set a purely standalone plan, and the stock has already re-rated about 46% off its CHF 5.83 low to near its 52-week high with no hard, dated event left to force the residual discount closed. The integration is only two quarters old; a soft first-half 2026 print, a vendor-incentive scare, a lumpy working-capital quarter that dents the cash-flow narrative, or a broad market de-grossing could send a near-52-week-high momentum name back toward CHF 6.5-7 quickly. Confirmation would be any of: a flat-to-down like-for-like revenue print in 2026, a fresh Microsoft incentive headwind, or a slip in the synergy run-rate.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is on which earnings number is real. The sell side anchors on the depressed accounting profit and cautious adjusted earnings per share — Deutsche Bank cut its target to CHF 7.90 citing a 'tougher setup around vendor incentives,' and a widely-followed model marks fair value near CHF 8.86 while slashing its net-margin assumption from 15.9% to 9.45%. That framing under-credits the cash. On enterprise value the business trades at about 1.2 times sales, roughly six to eight times free cash flow (an 11% free-cash-flow yield) and about 5.7 times adjusted EBITDA — a clear discount to the reseller peer cohort (Insight, Computacenter, Bechtle, CDW) at low-to-mid-teens cash-flow multiples — with roughly CHF 350 million of net cash the street mostly ignores, and a synergy program (CHF 86 million run-rate, ahead of plan) plus a 2030 margin path (adjusted EBITDA from about 21% toward 28%) that is under-modeled. Where we do NOT disagree, and this is the discipline: the street is right that GAAP profit is near zero, that Microsoft's rebate lever is a genuine and proven risk, and that the stock has already re-rated about 46% off its CHF 5.83 low to near its 52-week high — so the easy part of the gap is closed and what remains is a quality-adjusted discount, not a free lunch.
forcing_function: There is no hard, dated event left to force a re-rating — this is the crux of the timing call. The take-private catalyst is spent: the Bain/Apax/CVC pursuit resolved into the Crayon merger (completed 2025-07-02) and Bain publicly stepped away, and the Capital Markets Day (2026-06-09) already delivered a standalone 2030 plan (high-single-digit revenue growth, adjusted EBITDA above 28%, cash conversion above 60%). The remaining re-rating drivers are all soft and non-binding: proof of the 2026 margin guide (adjusted EBITDA above 23%) and continued synergy delivery toward the CHF 100 million run-rate at the first-half 2026 results (now dated 2026-08-26); and the dormant, undated optionality of a renewed private-equity approach, given the founders' 29% stake, their prior willingness to sell, and an active 2026 take-private market for European software. None of these is a firm, scheduled event with a contractual payout, so the honest read is a soft, non-binding catalyst rather than a hard, dated one.
valley_of_death: The near-term risk window runs to the first-half 2026 results, due 2026-08-26 (management-confirmed date, consistent with the anchor's ~46-day estimate). There is no financing valley — the company is net cash with no debt wall — so the risks are operational and mechanical. First, Microsoft vendor-incentive volatility: the enterprise-agreement-to-CSP transition powered the 2025 recovery, but incentive structures have surprised negatively before, and management's flat-out claim of 'no headwinds' in 2026 is a hostage to fortune. Second, execution slippage in the still-turning North America unit (revenue down 12.6% in 2025) and the exited Latin American markets. Third, GAAP optics: heavy integration and restructuring charges keep reported profit near zero, so a headline net loss could unsettle quality-focused holders even if cash flow is fine. Fourth, working-capital lumpiness — a reseller's quarterly free cash flow swings hard on receivables and payables timing (days-sales-outstanding and days-payable are both distorted by the agent/net-revenue accounting), so one weak quarter could dent the cash-flow narrative the whole thesis rests on. Fifth, the macro backdrop: the current regime carries several late-July to mid-August binaries (an AI-capital-spending earnings test, a tariff statutory cliff, a Middle East ceasefire clock) that could trigger broad forced-selling, and a momentum name trading near its 52-week high would give back fast in a de-grossing.
positioning_washout: There is no acute forced-selling trigger, but two soft overhangs. The founding/anchor shareholders (von Stockar, Gilli and the B. Curti group) hold roughly 29%; they are strategic holders who once sought a sale, so they are not mechanical sellers, but any future exit would be a supply event. Separately, the Crayon merger was paid partly in newly issued SoftwareOne shares, so some former Crayon holders are non-natural long-term owners who may sell into the recent strength toward 52-week highs — a slow, technical supply drag rather than a capitulation. There is no dividend-cut dynamic to force a yield-focused base out (the dividend is a token CHF 0.15) and no index-driven mechanical selling identified. Net: modest, not a washout to buy into.
moderator_conclusion: This is a genuinely cheap, cleanly financed business whose defining catalyst has already been spent, and that combination argues for patience rather than an aggressive entry. The value is real: about seven to eight times free cash flow with an 11% yield, roughly CHF 350 million of net cash, a credible margin-expansion runway (adjusted EBITDA from about 21% toward a 28% target by 2030) and synergies running ahead of plan — a clear discount to the reseller peers at low-to-mid-teens cash-flow multiples. But the special situation that made SoftwareOne interesting — the Bain/Apax/CVC take-private — resolved into the 2025 Crayon merger, the Capital Markets Day has already fired, and the stock has re-rated about 46% off its CHF 5.83 low to near its 52-week high with no hard, dated forcing function left to close the residual gap. In the current dispersion-and-hawkish regime that rewards hard-dated structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes (distressed, deleveraging, spinoffs, forced sellers), an already-re-rated operational turnaround with near-zero GAAP earnings, Microsoft-incentive dependence and a material longer-horizon AI overhang does not earn top sizing. The value case and the catalyst case both land at a moderate 3. The call is to wait for the wash-out: a soft first-half 2026 print, a vendor-incentive scare, or a broad market de-grossing that resets the stock toward CHF 6.5-7 would turn a roughly balanced risk/reward into a compelling one. Wait for that flush before committing capital.
sop_breakdown: Whole-company intrinsic plus net-cash overlay (no segment revenue block available for a true segment sum-of-the-parts). Operating business about CHF 8.9 per share — roughly 9-10 times sustainable free cash flow of about CHF 210-228 million, cross-checked at about 5.5-6 times 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about CHF 340-360 million, for an operating enterprise value near CHF 1.9 billion on roughly 215 million shares. Net cash about CHF 1.6 per share (roughly CHF 345-360 million: cash and short-term investments of CHF 434 million less CHF 74.5 million of lease debt). Sum about CHF 10.5 per share — above the cautious analyst cluster (CHF 7.9-8.9) and in line with the stock-page discounted-cash-flow fair value of CHF 10.8, below the cheaper earnings-power (EPV) reading.
risk_reward: From CHF 8.495: downside to the adverse case CHF 6.5 is about CHF 2.0 (roughly 23% down), upside to base-case fair value CHF 10.5 is about CHF 2.0 (roughly 24% up), and upside to the favorable case CHF 13.5 is about CHF 5.0 (roughly 59%). Roughly balanced to base, skewed favorably only to the bull case — an acceptable but not compelling setup at a near-52-week-high entry, which argues for waiting.
peer_comps_note: The peer file (Insight/NSIT, Computacenter/CCC.L, Bechtle/BC8.DE, CDW; verdict cheap versus peers) anchors on those resellers trading in the low-to-mid teens on free cash flow versus SoftwareOne at about seven to eight times — a wide gap. No the peer-group override or the anchor multiple is supplied, and convergence is not flagged as sector regulatory, so part of the gap is idiosyncratic rather than shared sector beta. But the discount is substantially quality-adjusted, not pure alpha: SoftwareOne carries near-zero GAAP earnings, a 0-of-7 beat record, contracting gross margin, Microsoft-incentive dependence and only two quarters of post-merger history, so a mid-single-digit cash-flow multiple discount to those peers is warranted. The peer note's own read — that the move toward 52-week highs 'likely reflects buyout/takeover speculation' — is now stale: the take-private saga resolved in the 2025 Crayon merger, so the recent strength is better explained by the synergy-driven operational re-rating than by a live bid.

bull_thesis:
SoftwareOne is a repaired business that the market is still pricing as a broken one, and the repair is now documented rather than promised. The company buys software licences and cloud capacity from vendors - overwhelmingly Microsoft, but also Amazon Web Services, Google and Adobe - and resells them to about 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers with advice and managed services wrapped around the transaction. In July 2025 it merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor with a large distribution arm, roughly doubling its size.

The first-half 2026 results, reported on 26 August 2026, are the evidence. Revenue grew 11.6% year on year on a like-for-like basis (comparing the merged company against what the two businesses did separately a year earlier), up from just 1.4% for full-year 2025. Adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, stated before one-off integration costs - reached 24.9% of revenue, a 4.5 percentage-point improvement in a year, with the second quarter alone at 28.9%. Every region grew and every business line grew, including North America, which had shrunk 12.6% in 2025. The entire cost-savings programme was delivered at the top of its CHF 80-100 million range six months early, at CHF 100 million of run-rate savings, and integration costs are now guided lower than first estimated, at CHF 75-85 million rather than CHF 80-100 million. Chief executive Raphael Erb described integration as 'substantially completed'.

Management also did the unglamorous thing it promised in March 2026: it narrowed the gap between its adjusted profit measure and its statutory one, from CHF 33 million of adjustments to CHF 18.4 million. That matters more than the headline margin, because the standing objection to this company was always that the adjusted number flattered a business that earned nothing on a reported basis. A reported EBITDA margin of 22.7% in the first half, up 5.2 percentage points, is now within touching distance of the adjusted figure.

Underneath the recovery sits a genuinely good business the market values at nothing in particular. The channel arm - selling through other resellers rather than direct to end customers - grew 35.6% in the first half at a 57.2% adjusted margin, and in February 2026 became, on the company's own account, the first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud, rolling out across ten markets with more to follow. That is a scalable, vendor-diversifying franchise growing three times as fast as the group, and management has just given its head a seat on the executive board. The services business is repairing in parallel, with its adjusted margin rising from 3.3% to 8.5% in a year on 17.4% growth, led by cloud migration, data and cybersecurity work.

On valuation the arithmetic is stark. At CHF 9.25 the equity is worth about CHF 1.99 billion; adding CHF 408 million of net debt gives an enterprise value near CHF 2.4 billion, or roughly 6.2 times the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA that the company's own 23-25% full-year margin guidance implies on about CHF 1.68 billion of 2026 revenue. Live peer multiples today are 9.0 times at ALSO Holding, 10.4 times at Bechtle, 13.1 times at Insight Enterprises and 13.7 times at CDW. On earnings the gap is just as wide: consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 puts the stock on under 11 times, against 18-23 times for the same peer group. Every single turn of enterprise-value-to-EBITDA re-rating is worth about CHF 1.85 a share.

The conditions this case depends on are specific and checkable. Microsoft's 5% margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint, effective October 2026, must prove as immaterial as Erb asserts. Second-half 2026 growth must decelerate only modestly from the four-percentage-point pull-forward tailwind management has already flagged. The 2027-28 step-up in capital spending to about 8% of revenue must genuinely be funded from released working capital rather than from shareholders. And cash conversion, which the chief financial officer put at 69% on the 26 August call - free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 against CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA, above the company's own 60% target and inside the 60-70% band the peer multiples assume - must hold there through the capital-spending step-up rather than sagging back. If those hold, a business earning CHF 0.85-1.00 per share by 2027-28 with a scaling distribution arm should not trade at ten times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The cheapness that put this stock on the screen was overstated by the screen and then understated by our own first correction of it. On the company's own figures the discount is real, so the bear case has to rest on what the next two years do to that cash rather than on a claim that it was never there.

Start with the number our file got wrong twice over. The screen carried CHF 585 million of trailing free cash flow and a 7.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, which is nonsense. But our first correction of it - to roughly CHF 117 million, a 5.9% yield and a 29% conversion rate - was also wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual cash-flow row and invented a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, given by chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August 2026 call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 - operating cash flow of CHF 271.6 million less CHF 71.9 million of capital spending - a 69% conversion of the CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA and above the company's own above-60% target. On the strict statement basis it is CHF 174.2 million. What survives from the original objection is narrower but still real: the screen's own figure is unusable because this balance sheet carries CHF 4.5 billion of receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of payables, so any single date's cash figure is a snapshot of supplier-payment timing, and full-year reseller cash flow captures the year-end float peak. The bear case is therefore about the durability of that 69%, not its existence.

Second, there is no net cash. Our prior note credited roughly CHF 350 million of it. The company reported net debt of CHF 408 million at 30 June 2026, up from CHF 369.3 million at the end of 2025; recomputed strictly from the balance sheet the figure is CHF 483 million. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million - a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolving credit facility - against CHF 383 million of cash, and roughly 36% of those borrowings, some CHF 311 million, fall due inside twelve months, more than the revolver draw alone. Behind the debt there is no book cushion: goodwill and acquired intangibles of CHF 1.89 billion exceed shareholders' equity of CHF 0.99 billion, so tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion. That is a statement about recovery in a liquidation, not a solvency signal - Schraner put leverage at 1.1 times on the same call, and the negative net working capital of minus CHF 509 million is the reseller model itself rather than distress. The bear objection here is price, not survival: in a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September, a mid-cap rolling CHF 311 million of near-dated, largely floating-rate borrowings on a net financial charge already running about CHF 52 million a year pays more for them than it did.

Third, the growth just reported is partly borrowed from the future. Erb conceded on the August call that early customer renewals ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase contributed 'around 4 percentage points' of the 11.6% first-half growth, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Strip the pull-forward and underlying growth is closer to 7-8%. The direct business - still the largest profit contributor - grew only 1.5% in the half and actually declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Fourth, the profit pool is set by a supplier, not by the company. Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management's answer - 'there is absolutely no material impact for us' - is an assertion with a hope attached, that reductions 'should largely be balanced by other incentive opportunity'. This is the same vendor whose previous incentive change produced a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America, and management sounded similarly relaxed going into that one.

Fifth, the cash-generation story gets worse precisely when the market expects it to get better. Capital spending rises to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28, roughly double the current run rate, to fund the automation that underwrites the 2030 margin ambition. The chief financial officer says the funding 'will come from the release of net working capital. So it should be in a way cash neutral.' Working capital can be released once; the spending recurs. On roughly CHF 1.8 billion of revenue that is CHF 130-145 million a year of capital spending against about CHF 75 million today - some CHF 60-70 million a year off free cash flow, which would take the CHF 211.7 million just reported down toward CHF 145-160 million through the investment years even if operating margins do everything management promises. The 69% conversion rate is a starting point, not a run rate.

Sixth, the statutory record remains poor and the multiple already reflects a recovery. Net income was CHF 21 million in 2023, minus CHF 2 million in 2024 and CHF 0.9 million in 2025; earnings per share have compounded at minus 70% a year over five years. The company has beaten earnings expectations in 2 of the last 7 quarters. And the market is no longer ignoring the turn: the stock gapped 9.5% higher on the results (CHF 8.65 to CHF 9.47 on 26 August 2026, on four times normal volume), sits 21% above its 200-day average and 92% of the way up its 52-week range after rising from a low of CHF 5.83.

Finally, the terminal question. Roughly half of revenue is a services business earning 8.5% - the economics of billing people's time at a spread, which is exactly the model artificial intelligence deflates. Management's own 2030 margin bridge is built on 'AI and automation efficiencies', which is another way of saying the work will need fewer people. A company can win that efficiency race internally and still lose the bill rates that came with selling the hours. Add hyperscalers and software vendors selling ever more directly through their own marketplaces, and the intermediary's long-run reason to exist is a live question rather than a settled one. What confirms this case: second-half 2026 growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, free cash flow for 2026 below CHF 175 million against the CHF 211.7 million just reported, or any commentary walking back the October Microsoft change as immaterial.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the recovery - the market saw that on 26 August and paid 9.5% for it - but about what the recovered business converts into cash.

The visible street position is internally inconsistent, and the inconsistency is instructive. The eleven analysts modelling revenue put 2027 at about CHF 1.74 billion; the ten modelling earnings put 2027 earnings per share at CHF 0.85 and 2028 at CHF 0.94. But the handful modelling EBITDA carry CHF 289 million for 2027 - a 16.6% margin, against a company guiding 23-25% and delivering 24.9% in the first half of 2026. Either those EBITDA estimates are stale pre-merger assumptions, or the analysts are quietly refusing to capitalise the adjusted measure. We think it is partly both, and that the refusal is more right than wrong.

Our own view sits between the two. The adjusted profitability is real as an operating result - the narrowing of adjustments from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million is the proof - but it converts to shareholder cash at well under half: after roughly CHF 41 million of interest, a guided 30% tax rate, and capital spending that management has told us doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28. Trailing free cash flow of about CHF 117 million is 29% of the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA the guidance implies. The peer multiples we are being invited to close the gap to attach to businesses converting at 60-70%. So the honest anchor is 12-13 times earnings, not 9-10 times EBITDA - which is exactly why we arrive at CHF 11.50 and not the CHF 15-plus the raw parts arithmetic produces.

Where the street is genuinely too bearish is the channel business. Nobody is valuing a line growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, newly authorised as Google Cloud's first global distributor and rolling out country by country, at anything other than the group multiple. Management just put its head on the executive board, which is where a company signals what it thinks it is becoming. That is the piece of this sum-of-the-parts the market is not pricing separately, and it is the reason a discount this wide should not persist indefinitely.

The specific street assumption we think is wrong in the other direction is the treatment of Microsoft's October 2026 margin reduction as a non-event because management called it 'absolutely no material impact'. The company said something similar before the last incentive change, which cost it a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America.
forcing_function:
There is no dated event that forces a re-rating, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. The re-rating trigger that existed - the delivery of the merger savings - fired on 26 August 2026 and the market paid for it the same day.

What remains is a sequence of scheduled proof points, each of which either extends or breaks the recovery narrative:
- Full-year 2026 results, due around the end of the first quarter of 2027 (the 2025 full year was reported on 31 March 2026). This is the one that matters. Three numbers decide it: where the full-year adjusted margin lands inside the 23-25% guide, whether the direct business returned to growth in the second half as management promised, and what free cash flow actually printed for the year against the CHF 117 million trailing figure.
- October 2026, when Microsoft's 5% partner-margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint takes effect. This is a dated risk event rather than a catalyst, and management has staked credibility on it being immaterial.
- The 2027-28 capital-spending programme, which will show up in cash-flow statements from the 2027 half-year onward and will settle the argument about whether adjusted profitability reaches shareholders.
- A residual and unhandicapped possibility: a business generating CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA with an integration completed, a scaling distribution arm and a market value under CHF 2 billion is the kind of asset that attracts strategic or private-equity attention. That was the story in 2023-24 and it failed. We do not underwrite it and it carries no weight in the conviction here.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where this thesis is most exposed, and the risks are dated rather than speculative.

The growth comparison turns immediately. Management disclosed on 26 August that roughly four percentage points of the 11.6% first-half growth came from customers renewing early ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Underlying growth is therefore nearer 7-8%, and the reported second-half number will look materially weaker than the first-half one for reasons that are arithmetic rather than operational. Investors who bought the 26 August print will be marking a slowdown.

Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management expects no material impact. If that proves optimistic it lands directly on the direct business, which is the largest profit contributor and which already grew only 1.5% in the first half and declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Cash is the pinch point rather than profit. Free cash flow was CHF 28.1 million in the first half of 2026 and roughly CHF 117 million over twelve months. Capital spending steps up to about 8% of revenue across 2027-28 - some CHF 130-145 million a year against roughly CHF 75 million today - funded, the chief financial officer says, 'from the release of net working capital'. Releasing working capital in a business whose current assets are CHF 4.5 billion of receivables means collecting faster or paying suppliers slower, and it can only be done once. There is no cash-burn hump in the equity-risk sense - the company is profitable - but there is a real risk that 2027 free cash flow prints near CHF 110-125 million and the market concludes the margin story never reaches the shareholder.

The balance sheet compounds this. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million (a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolver) against CHF 383 million of cash, with an interest bill running about CHF 41 million a year on largely floating-rate facilities. The current market regime is a tightening one - the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 58-60% to raise rates on 15-16 September 2026 after payrolls of 162,000 erased the prior soft print - with an oil shock running alongside it (Brent up 9.3% to about USD 96 over the 29-30 August weekend) and equity volatility printing below 14, which is complacency rather than comfort. A levered mid-cap with negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion and an Altman Z-score of 0.7 is not where you want to be holding when a complacent tape reprices. There is no near-term maturity wall we can identify from the materials - the bridge facility was repaid in January 2026 - but refinancing the term loan happens at higher rates than it was struck at.

One structural comfort worth naming: none of these risks are the market's shared risk. This thesis resolves on Microsoft's incentive policy and on the company's own cash conversion, not on oil, not on artificial-intelligence capital spending, and not on the rate path except through the interest bill. In a book where too many positions resolve on the same macro driver, that independence has value.
positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling in this name has largely already happened, which is a point in the stock's favour rather than against it.

Two forced-seller cohorts were created by the July 2025 Crayon merger. First, share count rose from about 152 million to about 217 million - roughly 65 million new shares issued to Crayon's holders, many of them Norwegian institutions and index funds that owned a Norwegian small-cap for Norwegian reasons and inherited a Swiss mid-cap. Any merger lock-up has long since lapsed, more than thirteen months on, and the drift of the shares through the first half of 2026 to a low of CHF 5.83 is consistent with that supply being worked off.

Second, the income buyers. The dividend has been roughly halved per share while the share count rose 43%: the company paid CHF 32.4 million in the first half of 2026 on about 215 million shares, some 15 centimes a share, against CHF 45.6 million in the first half of 2025 on about 152 million shares, some 30 centimes. For a Swiss mid-cap, income holders are a meaningful part of the register, and a halved per-share payout is exactly the trigger that forces a yield mandate to sell irrespective of value. That repricing sits behind the stock rather than in front of it.

What could still force selling is passive rather than active: a levered Swiss mid-cap that has run 59% off its low is a candidate for momentum and quality-factor flows in both directions, and average daily volume of about 526,000 shares against a CHF 2 billion market value means the register turns slowly. Today's print of CHF 9.25 came on roughly 125,000 shares, a quarter of normal - a thin tape, not conviction selling. The founder and anchor shareholders remain a large stable block, which cuts both ways: it dampens forced selling and it also means genuine free float is smaller than the market value suggests.
moderator_conclusion:
Take a starter position here rather than wait for CHF 8.00. That reverses our 31 August conclusion, and it reverses on our own arithmetic rather than on any news.

The business case is unchanged and remains well-evidenced. Six operational commitments made in March 2026 were kept or beaten by August: the full CHF 100 million of merger savings delivered six months early, North America returned to growth after a 12.6% contraction, integration costs guided below the original estimate, and - the one that speaks loudest about management quality - the gap between the adjusted and statutory profit measures narrowed from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million exactly as promised. Growth of 11.6% at a 24.9% adjusted margin, with every region and every line contributing, is a real recovery in a business that was drifting two years ago. Inside it sits a distribution arm growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin that the market values at the group multiple and probably should not.

What changed is the cash number, and it changed twice. The screen surfaced this name at 7.3 times free cash flow with an 11% yield and roughly CHF 350 million of net cash. The net cash was never there - the company reported CHF 408 million of net debt at 30 June 2026, CHF 483 million on a strict recomputation - and that correction stands. But our correction of the cash flow itself, to CHF 117 million on a 29% conversion rate, was wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual statement row and manufactured a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, from chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 - a 69% conversion of reported EBITDA, above its own 60% target - and CHF 174.2 million even on the strict statement basis.

That is decisive because the 29% conversion rate was the load-bearing leg of our own 26% haircut. We wrote that the peer multiples 'attach to businesses converting at 60-70%'. The company converts at 69%, inside that range. The other two haircut legs survive untouched - the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed, and consensus 2026-27 EBITDA of CHF 268-289 million sits well below the CHF 400 million the parts arithmetic capitalises - so the fair value is re-derived conservatively, on our own two published cross-checks with only the cash input replaced: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.09, and a 7.5% yield on CHF 211.7 million gives CHF 12.99 on 217.2 million weighted-average shares. The midpoint is CHF 12.05. The EBITDA anchor stays deliberately unrestored.

The adverse case moves for the same kind of reason. CHF 6.80 was our own parts figure of CHF 7.85 cut a further 13% on an Altman Z-score of 0.7 and negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion. Both numbers are arithmetically right and neither is a solvency signal for this balance sheet: the negative working capital is CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through payables, and leverage was reported at 1.1 times on the same call. The adverse case is the parts figure itself, CHF 7.85.

So the shape of the trade is not the one we described a week ago. Fair value is about 30% above CHF 9.25 and the adverse case about 15% below it - roughly two to one, against the balanced payoff we published and declined. Every reservation that made us wait is still live and none of it is priced away: growth decelerates in the second half on management's own four-percentage-point admission, Microsoft cuts partner margin from October 2026 on the largest profit line, capital spending doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 and will take free cash flow from CHF 211.7 million toward CHF 145-160 million while it runs, the stock sits 21% above its 200-day average after gapping 9.5% on results ten days ago, and some CHF 311 million of near-dated floating-rate borrowings refinances into a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September. That is why this is a starter rather than a full seat, and why conviction goes to four and not higher: the catalyst has already fired, no dated event ahead forces the re-rating, and the terminal question about a labour business in an artificial-intelligence deflation remains open.

What would take it higher: full-year 2026 free cash flow holding above CHF 200 million through the capital-spending step-up, or the October Microsoft change passing without a visible mark on direct-business growth. What would take it off: second-half growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, or 2026 free cash flow below CHF 175 million. And it remains a better trade below CHF 8.00, where the entry price meets the adverse case; we are simply no longer willing to insist on that level for a two-to-one payoff.

One caveat on verification, now largely closed. Our licensed feed returns no news and no press releases for this symbol between 1 August and 7 September 2026, and the only dated corporate event in that window - the executive board reorganisation effective 1 September - was pre-announced on the 26 August call. The drift from CHF 9.71 to CHF 9.25 was a thin tape, not an announcement.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, reconciling the favourable and adverse parts and then anchoring on cash rather than on adjusted profit. The parts, on about CHF 400 million of 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA (the level the company's 23-25% margin guidance implies on roughly CHF 1.68 billion of revenue), with the revenue split inferred from the disclosed first-half business-line margins because no segment table was supplied:
- Software and Cloud Direct, about CHF 285 million of EBITDA at 8 times: CHF 2,280 million. The largest profit contributor, growing only 1.5%, with its margin set by Microsoft's incentive policy - hence a discount to Bechtle's live 10.4 times.
- Channel, about CHF 135 million at 12 times: CHF 1,620 million. Growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud since February 2026, and the one part that deserves a premium to the group.
- Services, about CHF 75 million at 10 times: CHF 750 million. Margin repairing from 3.3% to 8.5%, but it is a labour business exposed to bill-rate deflation from artificial intelligence.
- Central and unallocated costs, about minus CHF 95 million capitalised at 9 times: minus CHF 855 million.
- Enterprise value from the parts: about CHF 3,795 million. Less net debt of CHF 450 million (the midpoint of the CHF 408 million the company reports at 30 June 2026 and the CHF 483 million recomputed from the balance sheet) gives equity of CHF 3,345 million, or about CHF 15.60 per share on 215 million shares.

We haircut that by roughly 26%, to CHF 11.50, for three stated reasons: the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed; the parts multiples attach to peers with positive tangible equity, where this balance sheet carries about minus CHF 0.9 billion of tangible book value, CHF 866 million of borrowings and an Altman Z-score of 0.7; and, decisively, adjusted EBITDA here converts to shareholder cash at about 29% (trailing free cash flow of roughly CHF 117 million) against the 60-70% the peer multiples assume, with capital spending set to double to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28.

Two independent cross-checks land in the same place: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.10, and a 7.5% yield on normalised free cash flow of roughly CHF 180 million gives CHF 11.60. CHF 11.50 implies about 7.4 times 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA - still a persistent discount to every peer, deliberately kept for the leverage and the single-vendor dependence.
risk_reward: From CHF 9.25 today, the adverse case sits at CHF 7.85 and the base-case fair value at CHF 12.05, with the favourable case at CHF 14.50. That is about 30% of upside against 15% of downside over an eighteen-month horizon - roughly two to one - on a 23% discount to fair value. There is no structural floor beneath the equity - no net cash, no deal terms, no tender offer - so the adverse case is a valuation level rather than a backstop, and it already assumes an orderly de-rating rather than a disorderly one. What moved the asymmetry is not the price but the cash figure the discount was being tested against: at a company-reported 69% conversion rate the discount is no longer explicable as a data artefact, and the payoff now earns a starter position instead of a wait. It would be better still below CHF 8.00, which is where the adverse case and the entry price meet.
peer_comps_note:
Peer multiples here were pulled live today rather than recalled, because reseller multiples move. On trailing twelve-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA the cohort reads: ALSO Holding 9.0 times, Bechtle 10.4 times, Insight Enterprises 13.1 times, CDW 13.7 times, with Computacenter at 15.1 times enterprise value to free cash flow (its EBITDA multiple is distorted). On earnings the group sits at roughly 18 times (Bechtle, CDW), 19 times (ALSO) and 23 times (Insight). SoftwareOne trades at about 6.2 times its 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA and under 11 times consensus 2027 earnings. The discount is real and it is large.

Three qualifications keep us from spending it all. First, SoftwareOne is not economically identical to the box-movers: its 25% adjusted margin on a much smaller revenue base reflects a licensing-and-services mix closer to Computacenter's than to ALSO's, which argues the right anchor is the middle of the cohort, not the bottom. Second, a meaningful part of the gap is credit-risk-justified rather than mispricing - tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion, the Altman Z-score is 0.7, and net debt is CHF 408-483 million, where Computacenter runs net cash and Bechtle just 1.2 times leverage. Third, and unlike a sector-wide de-rating, this gap is idiosyncratic: the peer cohort has not de-rated together, so the discount is name-specific and does carry genuine potential edge rather than shared sector beta. Closing even half the distance to Bechtle's 10.4 times is worth roughly CHF 4 a share, which is why the question is the durability of cash conversion, not whether the gap exists.
interrogator_dossier:
# SoftwareOne Holding AG (SWON.SW) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 7 September 2026 · **Listing:** SIX Swiss Exchange, quoted in Swiss francs (CHF)
**Price used throughout:** CHF 9.25 (latest quote, 7 September 2026; the last full close was CHF 9.71 on 4 September)
**Market value of the equity:** about CHF 1.99 billion on roughly 215 million shares
**Transcripts reviewed:** full-year 2025 results (31 March 2026) and first-half 2026 results (26 August 2026)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

SoftwareOne sells and manages other companies' software. It buys licences and cloud capacity from vendors — overwhelmingly Microsoft, but also Amazon Web Services, Google, Adobe and thousands of others — and resells them to some 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers, wrapping advice and managed services around the transaction. It earns a spread on the licence plus a fee on the work. In July 2025 it merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor with a large distribution arm, roughly doubling the company.

Across the two calls in front of us the story moves through three distinct chapters, and the movement is unusually clean.

**Chapter one — survival and repair (the March 2026 call, covering 2025).** The tone is apologetic in places and defensive throughout. Management's framing word is "transformational," but the substance is damage control: Microsoft cut the incentives it pays partners on Enterprise Agreements, and that cut ran straight through SoftwareOne's largest business. Full-year revenue on a like-for-like basis — comparing the merged company against what the two businesses did separately a year earlier — grew just 1.4%. North America shrank 12.6%, which co-chief operating officer Raphael Erb attributed to "previous GTM-related sales execution challenges," a phrase that concedes the problem was self-inflicted. Latin America shrank 4.4% and the company announced it was quitting four countries there. The proof points offered are process metrics, not results: CHF 43 million of cost savings achieved by year-end, a promise of CHF 80–100 million eventually.

**Chapter two — the hinge.** Buried in that same call is the fourth-quarter figure: revenue up 11% after three quarters of stagnation. Management flags it, but does not yet claim it as a trend — "the actions we are taking are working" is as far as they go.

**Chapter three — delivery (the August 2026 call, covering the first half of 2026).** The change in register is the single most striking thing in this file. Raphael Erb, now sole chief executive rather than co-chief operating officer, opens with "I'm proud of our performance." Like-for-like revenue growth is 11.6%. Adjusted profitability — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, stated before one-off integration costs, a measure known as adjusted EBITDA — reached 24.9% of revenue, up 4.5 percentage points in a year, with the second quarter alone at 28.9%. Every region grew and every business line grew. The CHF 100 million cost-savings target was hit at the top of the range, six months early, and integration is described as "substantially completed."

Two growth drivers were introduced and then genuinely delivered. The first is the conversion of customers from Microsoft Enterprise Agreements to the Cloud Solution Provider model — the same shift that was a headwind in 2025 became a tailwind in 2026, because the newer contracts bundle a service alongside the licence. The second is the channel business: selling through other resellers rather than direct to end customers. In February 2026 the company became, on its own account, "the first global authorized distributor for Google Cloud." That business grew 35.6% in the first half at a 57.2% adjusted margin.

One driver was quietly dropped, and it is worth naming because our prior note leaned on it. The special situation that first made this company interesting — the private-equity interest in taking it off the market during the 2023–24 governance fight — appears nowhere in either call. Neither analysts nor management raise it. The company has spent 2025 and 2026 doing the opposite of preparing for a sale: it issued roughly 65 million new shares to buy Crayon and levered its balance sheet to do so.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management's claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "We delivered 11.6% year-on-year revenue growth" (first half 2026, like-for-like) | Reported revenue rose 68.2% to CHF 818.3 million, but that number is inflated by consolidating Crayon from July 2025. The like-for-like figure is the honest one and it is corroborated by the regional detail, which sums consistently. | Supported |
| "Adjusted EBITDA margin of 24.9%, an improvement of 4.5 percentage points" | Cross-checks. Reported (unadjusted) profitability was 22.7%, and the gap of about CHF 18.6 million matches the CHF 18.4 million of stated adjustments. Management promised in March to "narrow the gap between the reported and adjusted" figure and has visibly done so. | Supported, and this is the strongest single piece of evidence in the file |
| "CHF 100 million of run rate cost synergies… the top end of the announced target 6 months ahead of schedule" | The trajectory is documented across both calls: CHF 43 million at end-2025, CHF 64 million by March 2026, CHF 100 million by August 2026. Integration costs came in *below* the original estimate (CHF 75–85 million expected versus CHF 80–100 million guided). | Supported and over-delivered |
| The implication that the business is generating strong cash | This is where the story is richer than the numbers. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow — operating cash flow less capital spending — is roughly CHF 117 million, not the CHF 585 million our screening feed carried. Our feed's figure, and the 7.3-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple derived from it, is an artefact of a reseller balance sheet that carries CHF 4.5 billion of receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of payables: the year-end snapshot flatters, the mid-year snapshot punishes. In the first half of 2026 the company converted CHF 54 million of profit into CHF 64.6 million of operating cash and CHF 28.1 million of free cash flow. | **Diverges materially. The deep-value screen that surfaced this name rests on a broken cash-flow number.** |
| "Net debt stood at CHF 408 million" (30 June 2026) | Correct, and it corrects a serious error in our own prior note, which described "roughly CHF 350 million of net cash." Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million (a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolving credit facility) against CHF 383 million of cash. Recomputed strictly from the balance sheet the figure is CHF 483 million; the company's CHF 408 million nets off other financial assets. Either way this is a liability, not a cushion. | **The single most important correction in this dossier** |
| "We are comfortable that we will land in the range… not at the bottom of the 23%" (full-year 2026 adjusted margin) | Half-year actual of 24.9% is already above the low end, and the second quarter ran at 28.9%. The guidance looks conservative rather than heroic. | Supported |
| The 2030 ambition of a 28%-plus adjusted margin | Long-dated and unfalsifiable today. The honest tell is the funding: chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner says capital spending rises to "8% of revenue" in 2027–28 to fund automation, "funded from the release of net working capital. So it should be in a way cash neutral." Working capital can only be released once; the spending recurs. | Unproven, and the funding logic is the weak joint |

The deeper forensic point sits underneath all of this. On a statutory basis SoftwareOne has earned almost nothing for three years running: net income of CHF 21 million in 2023, minus CHF 2 million in 2024, CHF 0.9 million in 2025. The trailing twelve-month figure through June 2026 is CHF 45.3 million, or 19 centimes of earnings per share. Meanwhile the adjusted operating measure implies roughly CHF 400 million of annual profitability. That gap — the distance between what the company asks you to look at and what actually reaches the bottom line — is the whole argument about this stock, and it is closing but has not closed.

The balance sheet reinforces the caution. Goodwill and acquired intangibles total CHF 1.89 billion against shareholders' equity of CHF 0.99 billion, meaning tangible book value is roughly *minus* CHF 0.9 billion. The Altman Z-score — a standard bankruptcy-distance measure where anything under 1.8 is the distress zone — reads 0.7. For a business with a CHF 5.2 billion current-asset float that number overstates the danger, but it correctly says there is no asset cushion beneath the equity.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, and sharply.**

*March 2026 (full-year 2025).* Hedged and process-focused. Melissa Mulholland: "This was a year where we delivered on our promises while building the foundation for further improvement" — the sentence structure of a management team asking for more time. Schraner on North America: "I'm very confident that in North America 2026, we will return into growth" — confidence expressed as a forecast rather than a fact. On impairments he is precise and defensive: LATAM written down by CHF 8 million, "based on what we know today, there are no further impairments expected."

*August 2026 (first half 2026).* Declarative. "I'm proud of our performance." "Integration is now substantially completed." "This clearly proves the key message from our Capital Markets Day. This is a very scalable business model." The North America promise made in March was kept and is stated as fact: "its second consecutive quarter of growth, up 8.6%."

The shift is from defensive vocabulary (efficiency, cost, discipline, adjustments) to offensive vocabulary (scalable, momentum, commercial execution, customer value creation). Erb's own line marks it: the company is moving "from integration towards customer focus and execution."

Specificity increased alongside confidence, which is the pattern that matters. Management now volunteers figures that cut against them — the four-percentage-point growth tailwind from pulled-forward renewals, the coming deceleration in the second half, the 42% statutory tax rate. A team hiding something does not hand analysts the deceleration number unprompted.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability score: High on operational commitments, Medium on the overall record.**

The tracked promises, March 2026 call to August 2026 call:

| Promised in March 2026 | Delivered by August 2026 |
|---|---|
| CHF 80–100 million of cost savings, timeline unstated but framed as multi-year | CHF 100 million achieved, six months early |
| Return to growth in North America in 2026, improvement visible in the first quarter | Second consecutive quarter of growth, up 8.6% in the half |
| Narrow the gap between reported and adjusted profitability | Gap narrowed to CHF 18.4 million from CHF 33 million |
| Integration costs of CHF 80–100 million | Now guided to CHF 75–85 million |
| No further impairments expected in 2026 | None taken in the first half |
| Growth weighted to the second half of the year | Missed in the right direction — growth arrived early, in the first half |

That is six commitments made and six kept or beaten inside five months. It is an unusually clean scorecard.

The counterweight is the longer record this management team inherited and partly owns. Our financial file shows the company beat earnings expectations in only 2 of the last 7 quarters, a 29% rate. Earnings per share have compounded at *minus* 70% a year over five years, from 76 centimes in 2021 to essentially zero in 2025. The 2022 loss, the 2024 loss and the governance turmoil of 2023–24 are all inside that window.

The resolution is that these are two different companies. The current chief executive took the top job with the merger; the operational promises made by *this* team have been kept. But an investor is buying an enterprise whose ten-year record includes a failed strategic review, a boardroom fight, a value-destroying period of drift and a bet-the-company acquisition. Five months of delivery earns a credibility upgrade, not absolution.

There is no sandbagging pattern in the classic sense, but there is deliberate conservatism: the full-year margin guide of 23–25% was left unchanged despite a first half at 24.9%, and Erb's explanation is candid rather than evasive — "the lower end of the range would require a scenario where several things would move against us at once. We are not seeing evidence of that today."

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring question is Microsoft, and it is asked at every call by a different person.** Florian Treisch of Kepler Cheuvreux in March: how much of a headwind or tailwind will the Enterprise Agreement incentive changes be? Christopher Tong of UBS in August: what about the 2027 incentive framework and the introduction of gross-margin caps? Andreas Wolf of Berenberg in March: what is the tailwind from Microsoft price increases? Analysts understand, correctly, that this is a business whose profit pool is set by a single supplier's compensation policy.

Management's August answer to Tong deserves scrutiny. Microsoft announced a 5% margin reduction from October 2026 on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint. Erb: "we would not expect a meaningful impact overall… there is absolutely no material impact for us on the incentive changes. We see them as very neutral." The double negative and the intensifier ("absolutely no material impact") are stronger than the evidence offered, which is that the affected products "make up only a small part of our overall CSP business" and that any reduction "should largely be balanced by other incentive opportunity" — a hope, not a contract. This is the same vendor whose last incentive change produced a full year of declining revenue in the direct business and a 12.6% contraction in North America. The pattern is worth remembering: in March 2026 management said of that earlier change, "we delivered better than expected." They said something similar going in.

**The second pressure point is the cost of the 2030 margin ambition.** Nooshin Nejati of Deutsche Bank pushed twice in August — "how much investments do you need to achieve this?" — and had to repeat the question after the first answer addressed something else. The eventual answer, that capital spending rises to about 8% of revenue and is funded by releasing working capital, is the most consequential disclosure on the call and it arrived only under repeat questioning.

**A topic analysts pushed on that later turned into news:** Wolf asked in March whether further impairments were possible beyond the CHF 8 million taken in Latin America. Management said no. None have appeared since, so this one resolved in management's favour.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody asked about the balance sheet in August — no question on the CHF 866 million of gross borrowings, the swing from a year-end cash position into CHF 408 million of net debt, the floating-rate exposure on a CHF 750 million facility in a tightening rate environment, or the covenant headroom beneath a negative tangible book value. Nobody asked about actual free cash flow as opposed to the "cash conversion ratio of 69%" that management chose to disclose. In a company this leveraged, that is the blind spot.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Statutory earnings remain nearly non-existent.** Net income of CHF 0.9 million in 2025 on CHF 1.24 billion of revenue. The trailing figure of CHF 45.3 million is better but still a 2.9% net margin.

🔴 **The screening case rests on a broken cash-flow figure.** The 7.3-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple and the 16.3% free-cash-flow margin that put this name in front of us are artefacts of receivables-and-payables timing. Real trailing free cash flow is about CHF 117 million, a yield near 5.9% rather than the double-digit figure implied.

🔴 **The balance sheet reversed and our prior note missed it.** From a reported year-end 2025 net-debt position of CHF 369.3 million to CHF 408 million at 30 June 2026, against negative tangible book value and an Altman Z-score of 0.7.

🔴 **Growth in the first half was flattered by roughly four percentage points** of customers renewing early ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price rise (Erb, August 2026: "the tailwind is around 4 percentage points"). Management has already told us the second half decelerates.

🔴 **Capital spending nearly doubles in 2027–28** to about 8% of revenue, funded by a one-time working-capital release. The cash-generation story gets worse before the margin story pays.

🔴 **Single-supplier dependence.** Microsoft sets the incentive framework that determines the profit pool, changes it unilaterally, and is changing it again in October 2026.

🔴 **The statutory tax rate ran at 42% in the first half**, guided to about 30% for the full year — a real drag between operating profitability and per-share earnings.

🟢 **Six operational commitments made in March 2026, six kept or beaten by August 2026.** The cost-savings target was hit at the top of the range six months early and integration costs came in below the original estimate.

🟢 **The gap between adjusted and reported profitability has narrowed sharply**, from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million. Management promised precisely this and delivered it. This is the antidote to the usual complaint about adjusted measures.

🟢 **Growth is broad-based.** Every region and every business line grew in the first half of 2026 — including North America, which was the wound of 2025, and Latin America, which the company had been exiting country by country.

🟢 **The channel business is a genuinely good asset hiding inside a mediocre one.** It grew 35.6% at a 57.2% adjusted margin and became the first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud in February 2026. It is scaling into new countries and it does not depend on Microsoft alone.

🟢 **The services business is repairing.** Adjusted margin rose from 3.3% to 8.5% in a year, and the work is increasingly attached to cloud migration and cybersecurity rather than licence administration.

🟢 **A long-running receivables problem closed.** The Crayon public-sector receivable in the Philippines began collecting in the first quarter of 2026, with USD 22 million received as of the March call.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of the merger changed.** In March, Crayon is spoken of as a project — integration, synergies, adjustments, costs. In August it is spoken of in the past tense: "Integration is now substantially completed with the company's focus shifting fully to commercial execution." Companies that are still struggling with an acquisition do not stop talking about it.

**Leadership consolidated, quietly.** March's call was fronted by two co-chief operating officers, Erb and Mulholland, alongside the chief financial officer. By August, Erb is chief executive and Mulholland is absent from the call. Erb also describes a reorganisation from seven reporting regions into three — Europe, the Americas and Asia-Pacific — and, tellingly, elevates the head of the channel business to the executive board. Where a company puts its board seats tells you where it thinks its future profit lives.

**Artificial intelligence is discussed as a customer, not as a threat.** Asked in March how AI model providers deal with resellers, Mulholland's answer is revealing: "Anthropic is certainly an area where we see additional partner opportunity as they need partners like us… we help guide our customers around which model makes sense." The company positions AI as more complexity to be navigated, and complexity is what it sells. That framing is plausible for the licensing business. It is much less plausible for the services business, where AI decouples billable output from headcount — and nobody on either call asked about that.

**The impairment answer was unusually precise.** Schraner in March: "we do the impairment test on CGU levels, which are the 7 regions… Otherwise, you would have impaired already at the end of 2025." That is a chief financial officer showing his work rather than deflecting, and it is the sort of detail that is easy to check later. It checked out.

**A number that does not tie.** The August transcript renders one integration-cost figure as "CHF 60.9 million of the total of CHF 18.4 million," which is arithmetically impossible and is almost certainly a transcription error for CHF 16.9 million. The surrounding figures — CHF 42.3 million cumulative, CHF 18.4 million of total adjustments — are internally consistent, so we treat the CHF 60.9 million as a transcript artefact rather than a disclosure problem. Flagged so nobody builds a model on it.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The operational trajectory has genuinely turned. A company that grew 1.4% with a 20.9% adjusted margin in 2025 grew 11.6% at a 24.9% margin in the first half of 2026, delivered its entire cost-savings programme six months early, fixed its worst region, and narrowed the distance between its adjusted and statutory numbers. That is not a story; it is a scorecard, and it is a good one.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this position:** the discount that makes this stock interesting is smaller than it looks, because the free-cash-flow figure the screen ran on is wrong and the net-cash position our prior note credited does not exist. Value SoftwareOne on the adjusted operating measure and it looks worth CHF 14–16 a share. Value it on the cash and statutory earnings that actually reach a shareholder — after CHF 41 million of interest on CHF 866 million of borrowings, a 30% tax rate, and capital spending that nearly doubles in 2027–28 — and it is worth CHF 11 or so against CHF 9.25 today. The gap between those two answers is the whole investment question, and it will be settled by cash conversion over the next eighteen months, not by the margin percentage.

**Moat.** Type: switching-costs, and shallow ones. The genuine stickiness comes from being embedded in a customer's licence estate — knowing what they own, what they over-bought, what renews when — and from being one of very few partners with true global reach across 70-plus countries and 10,000 vendors. Both Gartner and IDC rank the company a leader in software asset management. But the width has to be judged on returns, and the returns are ordinary: return on invested capital of 10.7%, return on equity of 1.8%, a gross margin the file marks as contracting, and a profit pool whose size is set annually by Microsoft rather than by SoftwareOne. That is **NARROW**, not wide.

The trend is the harder call. Adjusted margins are expanding fast, the channel business is scaling with real operating leverage, and the Google Cloud distribution authorisation genuinely widens the franchise beyond one vendor. Against that, Microsoft is cutting partner margins again from October 2026, and returns on capital have not yet risen enough to prove the merger created durable advantage rather than one-time cost savings. Cost synergies are not a moat. We call the trend **STABLE** — improving operationally, unchanged structurally — and would upgrade it only when returns on invested capital move durably above the mid-teens.

**Secular threat.** The structural risk here is not that businesses stop buying software. It is that artificial intelligence deflates the value of the labour that sits inside roughly half of this company's revenue. The services line grows 17% but earns only 8.5%, which is the economics of billing people's time at a spread — precisely the model where AI decouples output from headcount and compresses bill rates. Management's own answer points at it without meaning to: the 2030 margin bridge is built on "AI and automation efficiencies," which is another way of saying the work will need fewer people. A company can win that race internally and still lose the pricing that came with selling the hours. There is a second, adjacent risk: hyperscalers and software vendors selling ever more directly through their own marketplaces, which shrinks the intermediary's reason to exist.

Neither risk is terminal on today's evidence. The company is growing, gaining share in distribution, and being paid by vendors to manage a customer estate that is getting more complicated, not less. We rate the threat **material** — real enough to cap the multiple, not severe enough to make the cheapness a trap.

Which leaves the honest characterisation: this is not a fear-print on a melting business, and it is not a bargain hiding in plain sight either. It is a repaired, ordinary-quality intermediary at a fair-to-modest discount, whose cheapness on the screen was overstated by a data artefact and whose operating recovery is real, already partly recognised by the market, and not yet proven in cash.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
SoftwareOne is a repaired business that the market is still pricing as a broken one, and the repair is now documented rather than promised. The company buys software licences and cloud capacity from vendors - overwhelmingly Microsoft, but also Amazon Web Services, Google and Adobe - and resells them to about 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers with advice and managed services wrapped around the transaction. In July 2025 it merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor with a large distribution arm, roughly doubling its size.

The first-half 2026 results, reported on 26 August 2026, are the evidence. Revenue grew 11.6% year on year on a like-for-like basis (comparing the merged company against what the two businesses did separately a year earlier), up from just 1.4% for full-year 2025. Adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, stated before one-off integration costs - reached 24.9% of revenue, a 4.5 percentage-point improvement in a year, with the second quarter alone at 28.9%. Every region grew and every business line grew, including North America, which had shrunk 12.6% in 2025. The entire cost-savings programme was delivered at the top of its CHF 80-100 million range six months early, at CHF 100 million of run-rate savings, and integration costs are now guided lower than first estimated, at CHF 75-85 million rather than CHF 80-100 million. Chief executive Raphael Erb described integration as 'substantially completed'.

Management also did the unglamorous thing it promised in March 2026: it narrowed the gap between its adjusted profit measure and its statutory one, from CHF 33 million of adjustments to CHF 18.4 million. That matters more than the headline margin, because the standing objection to this company was always that the adjusted number flattered a business that earned nothing on a reported basis. A reported EBITDA margin of 22.7% in the first half, up 5.2 percentage points, is now within touching distance of the adjusted figure.

Underneath the recovery sits a genuinely good business the market values at nothing in particular. The channel arm - selling through other resellers rather than direct to end customers - grew 35.6% in the first half at a 57.2% adjusted margin, and in February 2026 became, on the company's own account, the first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud, rolling out across ten markets with more to follow. That is a scalable, vendor-diversifying franchise growing three times as fast as the group, and management has just given its head a seat on the executive board. The services business is repairing in parallel, with its adjusted margin rising from 3.3% to 8.5% in a year on 17.4% growth, led by cloud migration, data and cybersecurity work.

On valuation the arithmetic is stark. At CHF 9.25 the equity is worth about CHF 1.99 billion; adding CHF 408 million of net debt gives an enterprise value near CHF 2.4 billion, or roughly 6.2 times the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA that the company's own 23-25% full-year margin guidance implies on about CHF 1.68 billion of 2026 revenue. Live peer multiples today are 9.0 times at ALSO Holding, 10.4 times at Bechtle, 13.1 times at Insight Enterprises and 13.7 times at CDW. On earnings the gap is just as wide: consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 puts the stock on under 11 times, against 18-23 times for the same peer group. Every single turn of enterprise-value-to-EBITDA re-rating is worth about CHF 1.85 a share.

The conditions this case depends on are specific and checkable. Microsoft's 5% margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint, effective October 2026, must prove as immaterial as Erb asserts. Second-half 2026 growth must decelerate only modestly from the four-percentage-point pull-forward tailwind management has already flagged. The 2027-28 step-up in capital spending to about 8% of revenue must genuinely be funded from released working capital rather than from shareholders. And cash conversion, which the chief financial officer put at 69% on the 26 August call - free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 against CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA, above the company's own 60% target and inside the 60-70% band the peer multiples assume - must hold there through the capital-spending step-up rather than sagging back. If those hold, a business earning CHF 0.85-1.00 per share by 2027-28 with a scaling distribution arm should not trade at ten times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The cheapness that put this stock on the screen was overstated by the screen and then understated by our own first correction of it. On the company's own figures the discount is real, so the bear case has to rest on what the next two years do to that cash rather than on a claim that it was never there.

Start with the number our file got wrong twice over. The screen carried CHF 585 million of trailing free cash flow and a 7.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, which is nonsense. But our first correction of it - to roughly CHF 117 million, a 5.9% yield and a 29% conversion rate - was also wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual cash-flow row and invented a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, given by chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August 2026 call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 - operating cash flow of CHF 271.6 million less CHF 71.9 million of capital spending - a 69% conversion of the CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA and above the company's own above-60% target. On the strict statement basis it is CHF 174.2 million. What survives from the original objection is narrower but still real: the screen's own figure is unusable because this balance sheet carries CHF 4.5 billion of receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of payables, so any single date's cash figure is a snapshot of supplier-payment timing, and full-year reseller cash flow captures the year-end float peak. The bear case is therefore about the durability of that 69%, not its existence.

Second, there is no net cash. Our prior note credited roughly CHF 350 million of it. The company reported net debt of CHF 408 million at 30 June 2026, up from CHF 369.3 million at the end of 2025; recomputed strictly from the balance sheet the figure is CHF 483 million. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million - a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolving credit facility - against CHF 383 million of cash, and roughly 36% of those borrowings, some CHF 311 million, fall due inside twelve months, more than the revolver draw alone. Behind the debt there is no book cushion: goodwill and acquired intangibles of CHF 1.89 billion exceed shareholders' equity of CHF 0.99 billion, so tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion. That is a statement about recovery in a liquidation, not a solvency signal - Schraner put leverage at 1.1 times on the same call, and the negative net working capital of minus CHF 509 million is the reseller model itself rather than distress. The bear objection here is price, not survival: in a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September, a mid-cap rolling CHF 311 million of near-dated, largely floating-rate borrowings on a net financial charge already running about CHF 52 million a year pays more for them than it did.

Third, the growth just reported is partly borrowed from the future. Erb conceded on the August call that early customer renewals ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase contributed 'around 4 percentage points' of the 11.6% first-half growth, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Strip the pull-forward and underlying growth is closer to 7-8%. The direct business - still the largest profit contributor - grew only 1.5% in the half and actually declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Fourth, the profit pool is set by a supplier, not by the company. Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management's answer - 'there is absolutely no material impact for us' - is an assertion with a hope attached, that reductions 'should largely be balanced by other incentive opportunity'. This is the same vendor whose previous incentive change produced a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America, and management sounded similarly relaxed going into that one.

Fifth, the cash-generation story gets worse precisely when the market expects it to get better. Capital spending rises to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28, roughly double the current run rate, to fund the automation that underwrites the 2030 margin ambition. The chief financial officer says the funding 'will come from the release of net working capital. So it should be in a way cash neutral.' Working capital can be released once; the spending recurs. On roughly CHF 1.8 billion of revenue that is CHF 130-145 million a year of capital spending against about CHF 75 million today - some CHF 60-70 million a year off free cash flow, which would take the CHF 211.7 million just reported down toward CHF 145-160 million through the investment years even if operating margins do everything management promises. The 69% conversion rate is a starting point, not a run rate.

Sixth, the statutory record remains poor and the multiple already reflects a recovery. Net income was CHF 21 million in 2023, minus CHF 2 million in 2024 and CHF 0.9 million in 2025; earnings per share have compounded at minus 70% a year over five years. The company has beaten earnings expectations in 2 of the last 7 quarters. And the market is no longer ignoring the turn: the stock gapped 9.5% higher on the results (CHF 8.65 to CHF 9.47 on 26 August 2026, on four times normal volume), sits 21% above its 200-day average and 92% of the way up its 52-week range after rising from a low of CHF 5.83.

Finally, the terminal question. Roughly half of revenue is a services business earning 8.5% - the economics of billing people's time at a spread, which is exactly the model artificial intelligence deflates. Management's own 2030 margin bridge is built on 'AI and automation efficiencies', which is another way of saying the work will need fewer people. A company can win that efficiency race internally and still lose the bill rates that came with selling the hours. Add hyperscalers and software vendors selling ever more directly through their own marketplaces, and the intermediary's long-run reason to exist is a live question rather than a settled one. What confirms this case: second-half 2026 growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, free cash flow for 2026 below CHF 175 million against the CHF 211.7 million just reported, or any commentary walking back the October Microsoft change as immaterial.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the recovery - the market saw that on 26 August and paid 9.5% for it - but about what the recovered business converts into cash.

The visible street position is internally inconsistent, and the inconsistency is instructive. The eleven analysts modelling revenue put 2027 at about CHF 1.74 billion; the ten modelling earnings put 2027 earnings per share at CHF 0.85 and 2028 at CHF 0.94.
