This is the priced scenario materialising, not a new surprise, and it confirms rather than changes the interest-bill risk already carried above; no dated fact has emerged that changes the entry case, so no number in this record moves on it.]
positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling in this name has largely already happened, which is a point in the stock's favour rather than against it.

Two forced-seller cohorts were created by the July 2025 Crayon merger. First, share count rose from about 152 million to about 217 million - roughly 65 million new shares issued to Crayon's holders, many of them Norwegian institutions and index funds that owned a Norwegian small-cap for Norwegian reasons and inherited a Swiss mid-cap. Any merger lock-up has long since lapsed, more than thirteen months on, and the drift of the shares through the first half of 2026 to a low of CHF 5.83 is consistent with that supply being worked off.

Second, the income buyers. The dividend has been roughly halved per share while the share count rose 43%: the company paid CHF 32.4 million in the first half of 2026 on about 215 million shares, some 15 centimes a share, against CHF 45.6 million in the first half of 2025 on about 152 million shares, some 30 centimes. For a Swiss mid-cap, income holders are a meaningful part of the register, and a halved per-share payout is exactly the trigger that forces a yield mandate to sell irrespective of value. That repricing sits behind the stock rather than in front of it.

What could still force selling is passive rather than active: a levered Swiss mid-cap that has run 59% off its low is a candidate for momentum and quality-factor flows in both directions, and average daily volume of about 526,000 shares against a CHF 2 billion market value means the register turns slowly. Today's print of CHF 9.25 came on roughly 125,000 shares, a quarter of normal - a thin tape, not conviction selling. The founder and anchor shareholders remain a large stable block, which cuts both ways: it dampens forced selling and it also means genuine free float is smaller than the market value suggests.

[2026-09-29 delta check: the 2026-09-29 print (CHF 8.595) came on 70,149 shares, roughly 13% of the ~526,000-share average - an even thinner tape than the quarter-normal print described above, and again with no identifiable company news. This continues to read as drift, not conviction selling, and does not change the washout picture above.]
moderator_conclusion:
Take a starter position here rather than wait for CHF 8.00. That reverses our 31 August conclusion, and it reverses on our own arithmetic rather than on any news.

The business case is unchanged and remains well-evidenced. Six operational commitments made in March 2026 were kept or beaten by August: the full CHF 100 million of merger savings delivered six months early, North America returned to growth after a 12.6% contraction, integration costs guided below the original estimate, and - the one that speaks loudest about management quality - the gap between the adjusted and statutory profit measures narrowed from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million exactly as promised. Growth of 11.6% at a 24.9% adjusted margin, with every region and every line contributing, is a real recovery in a business that was drifting two years ago. Inside it sits a distribution arm growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin that the market values at the group multiple and probably should not.

What changed is the cash number, and it changed twice. The screen surfaced this name at 7.3 times free cash flow with an 11% yield and roughly CHF 350 million of net cash. The net cash was never there - the company reported CHF 408 million of net debt at 30 June 2026, CHF 483 million on a strict recomputation - and that correction stands. But our correction of the cash flow itself, to CHF 117 million on a 29% conversion rate, was wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual statement row and manufactured a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, from chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 - a 69% conversion of reported EBITDA, above its own 60% target - and CHF 174.2 million even on the strict statement basis.

That is decisive because the 29% conversion rate was the load-bearing leg of our own 26% haircut. We wrote that the peer multiples 'attach to businesses converting at 60-70%'. The company converts at 69%, inside that range. The other two haircut legs survive untouched - the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed, and consensus 2026-27 EBITDA of CHF 268-289 million sits well below the CHF 400 million the parts arithmetic capitalises - so the fair value is re-derived conservatively, on our own two published cross-checks with only the cash input replaced: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.09, and a 7.5% yield on CHF 211.7 million gives CHF 12.99 on 217.2 million weighted-average shares. The midpoint is CHF 12.05. The EBITDA anchor stays deliberately unrestored.

The adverse case moves for the same kind of reason. CHF 6.80 was our own parts figure of CHF 7.85 cut a further 13% on an Altman Z-score of 0.7 and negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion. Both numbers are arithmetically right and neither is a solvency signal for this balance sheet: the negative working capital is CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through payables, and leverage was reported at 1.1 times on the same call. The adverse case is the parts figure itself, CHF 7.85.

So the shape of the trade is not the one we described a week ago. Fair value is about 30% above CHF 9.25 and the adverse case about 15% below it - roughly two to one, against the balanced payoff we published and declined. Every reservation that made us wait is still live and none of it is priced away: growth decelerates in the second half on management's own four-percentage-point admission, Microsoft cuts partner margin from October 2026 on the largest profit line, capital spending doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 and will take free cash flow from CHF 211.7 million toward CHF 145-160 million while it runs, the stock sits 21% above its 200-day average after gapping 9.5% on results ten days ago, and some CHF 311 million of near-dated floating-rate borrowings refinances into a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September. That is why this is a starter rather than a full seat, and why conviction goes to four and not higher: the catalyst has already fired, no dated event ahead forces the re-rating, and the terminal question about a labour business in an artificial-intelligence deflation remains open.

What would take it higher: full-year 2026 free cash flow holding above CHF 200 million through the capital-spending step-up, or the October Microsoft change passing without a visible mark on direct-business growth. What would take it off: second-half growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, or 2026 free cash flow below CHF 175 million. And it remains a better trade below CHF 8.00, where the entry price meets the adverse case; we are simply no longer willing to insist on that level for a two-to-one payoff.

One caveat on verification, now largely closed. Our licensed feed returns no news and no press releases for this symbol between 1 August and 7 September 2026, and the only dated corporate event in that window - the executive board reorganisation effective 1 September - was pre-announced on the 26 August call. The drift from CHF 9.71 to CHF 9.25 was a thin tape, not an announcement.

[2026-09-29 delta check: the shares have drifted further, to CHF 8.595, again on a thin tape (70,149 shares vs a ~526,000 average) with no identifiable company news, per FMP's news/press-release feeds (checked through 2026-09-29) and a WebSearch pass. That widens the payoff described above to roughly 40% upside to the CHF 12.02 base case against about 9% downside to the CHF 7.85 adverse case - closer to 4.6 to 1 - purely on price, with every reservation in this record still live and unresolved: the Microsoft margin change is now two days out, the Fed's mid-September hike that this record carried as ~60% priced has occurred and been confirmed (with more hikes now flagged in the SEP dots), and second-half growth deceleration and the 2027-28 capex step-up remain ahead. None of that is a dated fact that moves fair value, downside price, upside price or conviction; the verdict, conviction and value-only conviction are carried unchanged from the 2026-09-22 anchor.]
sop_breakdown:
Base case, reconciling the favourable and adverse parts and then anchoring on cash rather than on adjusted profit. The parts, on about CHF 400 million of 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA (the level the company's 23-25% margin guidance implies on roughly CHF 1.68 billion of revenue), with the revenue split inferred from the disclosed first-half business-line margins because no segment table was supplied:
- Software and Cloud Direct, about CHF 285 million of EBITDA at 8 times: CHF 2,280 million. The largest profit contributor, growing only 1.5%, with its margin set by Microsoft's incentive policy - hence a discount to Bechtle's live 10.4 times.
- Channel, about CHF 135 million at 12 times: CHF 1,620 million. Growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud since February 2026, and the one part that deserves a premium to the group.
- Services, about CHF 75 million at 10 times: CHF 750 million. Margin repairing from 3.3% to 8.5%, but it is a labour business exposed to bill-rate deflation from artificial intelligence.
- Central and unallocated costs, about minus CHF 95 million capitalised at 9 times: minus CHF 855 million.
- Enterprise value from the parts: about CHF 3,795 million. Less net debt of CHF 450 million (the midpoint of the CHF 408 million the company reports at 30 June 2026 and the CHF 483 million recomputed from the balance sheet) gives equity of CHF 3,345 million, or about CHF 15.60 per share on 215 million shares.

We haircut that by roughly 26%, to CHF 11.50, for three stated reasons: the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed; the parts multiples attach to peers with positive tangible equity, where this balance sheet carries about minus CHF 0.9 billion of tangible book value, CHF 866 million of borrowings and an Altman Z-score of 0.7; and, decisively, adjusted EBITDA here converts to shareholder cash at about 29% (trailing free cash flow of roughly CHF 117 million) against the 60-70% the peer multiples assume, with capital spending set to double to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28.

Two independent cross-checks land in the same place: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.10, and a 7.5% yield on normalised free cash flow of roughly CHF 180 million gives CHF 11.60. CHF 11.50 implies about 7.4 times 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA - still a persistent discount to every peer, deliberately kept for the leverage and the single-vendor dependence.
risk_reward: From CHF 8.60 today (2026-09-29 quote, vs CHF 9.25 at the 2026-09-22 anchor), the adverse case sits at CHF 7.85 and the base-case fair value at CHF 12.02, with the favourable case at CHF 14.50. That is now about 40% of upside against roughly 9% of downside over an eighteen-month horizon - a payoff of about 4.6 to 1, wider than the two-to-one this record has been carrying, purely because the shares drifted lower (on a thin 70,149-share print, versus a roughly 526,000-share average, with no identifiable company news) while the fair-value and adverse-case levels are unchanged. There is no structural floor beneath the equity - no net cash, no deal terms, no tender offer - so the adverse case is a valuation level rather than a backstop, and it already assumes an orderly de-rating rather than a disorderly one. The discount to fair value is now wider than it was at the anchor, not because the case improved but because the entry got cheaper; the underlying reservations (Microsoft's October 2026 margin cut, second-half growth deceleration, the 2027-28 capital-spending step-up, the near-dated floating-rate refinancing) are all still live and none of them is priced away.
peer_comps_note:
Peer multiples here were pulled live today rather than recalled, because reseller multiples move. On trailing twelve-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA the cohort reads: ALSO Holding 9.0 times, Bechtle 10.4 times, Insight Enterprises 13.1 times, CDW 13.7 times, with Computacenter at 15.1 times enterprise value to free cash flow (its EBITDA multiple is distorted). On earnings the group sits at roughly 18 times (Bechtle, CDW), 19 times (ALSO) and 23 times (Insight). SoftwareOne trades at about 6.2 times its 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA and under 11 times consensus 2027 earnings. The discount is real and it is large.

Three qualifications keep us from spending it all. First, SoftwareOne is not economically identical to the box-movers: its 25% adjusted margin on a much smaller revenue base reflects a licensing-and-services mix closer to Computacenter's than to ALSO's, which argues the right anchor is the middle of the cohort, not the bottom. Second, a meaningful part of the gap is credit-risk-justified rather than mispricing - tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion, the Altman Z-score is 0.7, and net debt is CHF 408-483 million, where Computacenter runs net cash and Bechtle just 1.2 times leverage. Third, and unlike a sector-wide de-rating, this gap is idiosyncratic: the peer cohort has not de-rated together, so the discount is name-specific and does carry genuine potential edge rather than shared sector beta. Closing even half the distance to Bechtle's 10.4 times is worth roughly CHF 4 a share, which is why the question is the durability of cash conversion, not whether the gap exists.

bull_thesis:
SoftwareOne is a repaired business that the market is still pricing as a broken one, and the repair is now documented rather than promised. The company buys software licences and cloud capacity from vendors - overwhelmingly Microsoft, but also Amazon Web Services, Google and Adobe - and resells them to about 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers with advice and managed services wrapped around the transaction. In July 2025 it merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor with a large distribution arm, roughly doubling its size.

The first-half 2026 results, reported on 26 August 2026, are the evidence. Revenue grew 11.6% year on year on a like-for-like basis (comparing the merged company against what the two businesses did separately a year earlier), up from just 1.4% for full-year 2025. Adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, stated before one-off integration costs - reached 24.9% of revenue, a 4.5 percentage-point improvement in a year, with the second quarter alone at 28.9%. Every region grew and every business line grew, including North America, which had shrunk 12.6% in 2025. The entire cost-savings programme was delivered at the top of its CHF 80-100 million range six months early, at CHF 100 million of run-rate savings, and integration costs are now guided lower than first estimated, at CHF 75-85 million rather than CHF 80-100 million. Chief executive Raphael Erb described integration as 'substantially completed'.

Management also did the unglamorous thing it promised in March 2026: it narrowed the gap between its adjusted profit measure and its statutory one, from CHF 33 million of adjustments to CHF 18.4 million. That matters more than the headline margin, because the standing objection to this company was always that the adjusted number flattered a business that earned nothing on a reported basis. A reported EBITDA margin of 22.7% in the first half, up 5.2 percentage points, is now within touching distance of the adjusted figure.

Underneath the recovery sits a genuinely good business the market values at nothing in particular. The channel arm - selling through other resellers rather than direct to end customers - grew 35.6% in the first half at a 57.2% adjusted margin, and in February 2026 became, on the company's own account, the first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud, rolling out across ten markets with more to follow. That is a scalable, vendor-diversifying franchise growing three times as fast as the group, and management has just given its head a seat on the executive board. The services business is repairing in parallel, with its adjusted margin rising from 3.3% to 8.5% in a year on 17.4% growth, led by cloud migration, data and cybersecurity work.

On valuation the arithmetic is stark. At CHF 9.25 the equity is worth about CHF 1.99 billion; adding CHF 408 million of net debt gives an enterprise value near CHF 2.4 billion, or roughly 6.2 times the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA that the company's own 23-25% full-year margin guidance implies on about CHF 1.68 billion of 2026 revenue. Live peer multiples today are 9.0 times at ALSO Holding, 10.4 times at Bechtle, 13.1 times at Insight Enterprises and 13.7 times at CDW. On earnings the gap is just as wide: consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 puts the stock on under 11 times, against 18-23 times for the same peer group. Every single turn of enterprise-value-to-EBITDA re-rating is worth about CHF 1.85 a share.

The conditions this case depends on are specific and checkable. Microsoft's 5% margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint, effective October 2026, must prove as immaterial as Erb asserts. Second-half 2026 growth must decelerate only modestly from the four-percentage-point pull-forward tailwind management has already flagged. The 2027-28 step-up in capital spending to about 8% of revenue must genuinely be funded from released working capital rather than from shareholders. And cash conversion, which the chief financial officer put at 69% on the 26 August call - free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 against CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA, above the company's own 60% target and inside the 60-70% band the peer multiples assume - must hold there through the capital-spending step-up rather than sagging back. If those hold, a business earning CHF 0.85-1.00 per share by 2027-28 with a scaling distribution arm should not trade at ten times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The cheapness that put this stock on the screen was overstated by the screen and then understated by our own first correction of it. On the company's own figures the discount is real, so the bear case has to rest on what the next two years do to that cash rather than on a claim that it was never there.

Start with the number our file got wrong twice over. The screen carried CHF 585 million of trailing free cash flow and a 7.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, which is nonsense. But our first correction of it - to roughly CHF 117 million, a 5.9% yield and a 29% conversion rate - was also wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual cash-flow row and invented a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, given by chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August 2026 call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 - operating cash flow of CHF 271.6 million less CHF 71.9 million of capital spending - a 69% conversion of the CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA and above the company's own above-60% target. On the strict statement basis it is CHF 174.2 million. What survives from the original objection is narrower but still real: the screen's own figure is unusable because this balance sheet carries CHF 4.5 billion of receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of payables, so any single date's cash figure is a snapshot of supplier-payment timing, and full-year reseller cash flow captures the year-end float peak. The bear case is therefore about the durability of that 69%, not its existence.

Second, there is no net cash. Our prior note credited roughly CHF 350 million of it. The company reported net debt of CHF 408 million at 30 June 2026, up from CHF 369.3 million at the end of 2025; recomputed strictly from the balance sheet the figure is CHF 483 million. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million - a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolving credit facility - against CHF 383 million of cash, and roughly 36% of those borrowings, some CHF 311 million, fall due inside twelve months, more than the revolver draw alone. Behind the debt there is no book cushion: goodwill and acquired intangibles of CHF 1.89 billion exceed shareholders' equity of CHF 0.99 billion, so tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion. That is a statement about recovery in a liquidation, not a solvency signal - Schraner put leverage at 1.1 times on the same call, and the negative net working capital of minus CHF 509 million is the reseller model itself rather than distress. The bear objection here is price, not survival: in a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September, a mid-cap rolling CHF 311 million of near-dated, largely floating-rate borrowings on a net financial charge already running about CHF 52 million a year pays more for them than it did.

Third, the growth just reported is partly borrowed from the future. Erb conceded on the August call that early customer renewals ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase contributed 'around 4 percentage points' of the 11.6% first-half growth, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Strip the pull-forward and underlying growth is closer to 7-8%. The direct business - still the largest profit contributor - grew only 1.5% in the half and actually declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Fourth, the profit pool is set by a supplier, not by the company. Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management's answer - 'there is absolutely no material impact for us' - is an assertion with a hope attached, that reductions 'should largely be balanced by other incentive opportunity'. This is the same vendor whose previous incentive change produced a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America, and management sounded similarly relaxed going into that one.

Fifth, the cash-generation story gets worse precisely when the market expects it to get better. Capital spending rises to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28, roughly double the current run rate, to fund the automation that underwrites the 2030 margin ambition. The chief financial officer says the funding 'will come from the release of net working capital. So it should be in a way cash neutral.' Working capital can be released once; the spending recurs. On roughly CHF 1.8 billion of revenue that is CHF 130-145 million a year of capital spending against about CHF 75 million today - some CHF 60-70 million a year off free cash flow, which would take the CHF 211.7 million just reported down toward CHF 145-160 million through the investment years even if operating margins do everything management promises. The 69% conversion rate is a starting point, not a run rate.

Sixth, the statutory record remains poor and the multiple already reflects a recovery. Net income was CHF 21 million in 2023, minus CHF 2 million in 2024 and CHF 0.9 million in 2025; earnings per share have compounded at minus 70% a year over five years. The company has beaten earnings expectations in 2 of the last 7 quarters. And the market is no longer ignoring the turn: the stock gapped 9.5% higher on the results (CHF 8.65 to CHF 9.47 on 26 August 2026, on four times normal volume), sits 21% above its 200-day average and 92% of the way up its 52-week range after rising from a low of CHF 5.83.

Finally, the terminal question. Roughly half of revenue is a services business earning 8.5% - the economics of billing people's time at a spread, which is exactly the model artificial intelligence deflates. Management's own 2030 margin bridge is built on 'AI and automation efficiencies', which is another way of saying the work will need fewer people. A company can win that efficiency race internally and still lose the bill rates that came with selling the hours. Add hyperscalers and software vendors selling ever more directly through their own marketplaces, and the intermediary's long-run reason to exist is a live question rather than a settled one. What confirms this case: second-half 2026 growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, free cash flow for 2026 below CHF 175 million against the CHF 211.7 million just reported, or any commentary walking back the October Microsoft change as immaterial.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the recovery - the market saw that on 26 August and paid 9.5% for it - but about what the recovered business converts into cash.

The visible street position is internally inconsistent, and the inconsistency is instructive. The eleven analysts modelling revenue put 2027 at about CHF 1.74 billion; the ten modelling earnings put 2027 earnings per share at CHF 0.85 and 2028 at CHF 0.94. But the handful modelling EBITDA carry CHF 289 million for 2027 - a 16.6% margin, against a company guiding 23-25% and delivering 24.9% in the first half of 2026. Either those EBITDA estimates are stale pre-merger assumptions, or the analysts are quietly refusing to capitalise the adjusted measure. We think it is partly both, and that the refusal is more right than wrong.

Our own view sits between the two. The adjusted profitability is real as an operating result - the narrowing of adjustments from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million is the proof - but it converts to shareholder cash at well under half: after roughly CHF 41 million of interest, a guided 30% tax rate, and capital spending that management has told us doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28. Trailing free cash flow of about CHF 117 million is 29% of the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA the guidance implies. The peer multiples we are being invited to close the gap to attach to businesses converting at 60-70%. So the honest anchor is 12-13 times earnings, not 9-10 times EBITDA - which is exactly why we arrive at CHF 11.50 and not the CHF 15-plus the raw parts arithmetic produces.

Where the street is genuinely too bearish is the channel business. Nobody is valuing a line growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, newly authorised as Google Cloud's first global distributor and rolling out country by country, at anything other than the group multiple. Management just put its head on the executive board, which is where a company signals what it thinks it is becoming. That is the piece of this sum-of-the-parts the market is not pricing separately, and it is the reason a discount this wide should not persist indefinitely.

The specific street assumption we think is wrong in the other direction is the treatment of Microsoft's October 2026 margin reduction as a non-event because management called it 'absolutely no material impact'. The company said something similar before the last incentive change, which cost it a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America.
forcing_function:
There is no dated event that forces a re-rating, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. The re-rating trigger that existed - the delivery of the merger savings - fired on 26 August 2026 and the market paid for it the same day.

What remains is a sequence of scheduled proof points, each of which either extends or breaks the recovery narrative:
- Full-year 2026 results, due around the end of the first quarter of 2027 (the 2025 full year was reported on 31 March 2026). This is the one that matters. Three numbers decide it: where the full-year adjusted margin lands inside the 23-25% guide, whether the direct business returned to growth in the second half as management promised, and what free cash flow actually printed for the year against the CHF 117 million trailing figure.
- October 2026, when Microsoft's 5% partner-margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint takes effect. This is a dated risk event rather than a catalyst, and management has staked credibility on it being immaterial. It is now two days away.
- The 2027-28 capital-spending programme, which will show up in cash-flow statements from the 2027 half-year onward and will settle the argument about whether adjusted profitability reaches shareholders.
- A residual and unhandicapped possibility: a business generating CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA with an integration completed, a scaling distribution arm and a market value under CHF 2 billion is the kind of asset that attracts strategic or private-equity attention. That was the story in 2023-24 and it failed. We do not underwrite it and it carries no weight in the conviction here.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where this thesis is most exposed, and the risks are dated rather than speculative.

The growth comparison turns immediately. Management disclosed on 26 August that roughly four percentage points of the 11.6% first-half growth came from customers renewing early ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Underlying growth is therefore nearer 7-8%, and the reported second-half number will look materially weaker than the first-half one for reasons that are arithmetic rather than operational. Investors who bought the 26 August print will be marking a slowdown.

Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management expects no material impact. If that proves optimistic it lands directly on the direct business, which is the largest profit contributor and which already grew only 1.5% in the first half and declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Cash is the pinch point rather than profit. Free cash flow was CHF 28.1 million in the first half of 2026 and roughly CHF 117 million over twelve months. Capital spending steps up to about 8% of revenue across 2027-28 - some CHF 130-145 million a year against roughly CHF 75 million today - funded, the chief financial officer says, 'from the release of net working capital'. Releasing working capital in a business whose current assets are CHF 4.5 billion of receivables means collecting faster or paying suppliers slower, and it can only be done once. There is no cash-burn hump in the equity-risk sense - the company is profitable - but there is a real risk that 2027 free cash flow prints near CHF 110-125 million and the market concludes the margin story never reaches the shareholder.

The balance sheet compounds this. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million (a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolver) against CHF 383 million of cash, with an interest bill running about CHF 41 million a year on largely floating-rate facilities. The current market regime is a tightening one - the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 58-60% to raise rates on 15-16 September 2026 after payrolls of 162,000 erased the prior soft print - with an oil shock running alongside it (Brent up 9.3% to about USD 96 over the 29-30 August weekend) and equity volatility printing below 14, which is complacency rather than comfort. A levered mid-cap with negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion and an Altman Z-score of 0.7 is not where you want to be holding when a complacent tape reprices. There is no near-term maturity wall we can identify from the materials - the bridge facility was repaid in January 2026 - but refinancing the term loan happens at higher rates than it was struck at.

One structural comfort worth naming: none of these risks are the market's shared risk. This thesis resolves on Microsoft's incentive policy and on the company's own cash conversion, not on oil, not on artificial-intelligence capital spending, and not on the rate path except through the interest bill. In a book where too many positions resolve on the same macro driver, that independence has value.

positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling in this name has largely already happened, which is a point in the stock's favour rather than against it.

Two forced-seller cohorts were created by the July 2025 Crayon merger. First, share count rose from about 152 million to about 217 million - roughly 65 million new shares issued to Crayon's holders, many of them Norwegian institutions and index funds that owned a Norwegian small-cap for Norwegian reasons and inherited a Swiss mid-cap. Any merger lock-up has long since lapsed, more than thirteen months on, and the drift of the shares through the first half of 2026 to a low of CHF 5.83 is consistent with that supply being worked off.

Second, the income buyers. The dividend has been roughly halved per share while the share count rose 43%: the company paid CHF 32.4 million in the first half of 2026 on about 215 million shares, some 15 centimes a share, against CHF 45.6 million in the first half of 2025 on about 152 million shares, some 30 centimes. For a Swiss mid-cap, income holders are a meaningful part of the register, and a halved per-share payout is exactly the trigger that forces a yield mandate to sell irrespective of value. That repricing sits behind the stock rather than in front of it.

What could still force selling is passive rather than active: a levered Swiss mid-cap that has run 59% off its low is a candidate for momentum and quality-factor flows in both directions, and average daily volume of about 526,000 shares against a CHF 2 billion market value means the register turns slowly. Today's print of CHF 9.25 came on roughly 125,000 shares, a quarter of normal - a thin tape, not conviction selling. The founder and anchor shareholders remain a large stable block, which cuts both ways: it dampens forced selling and it also means genuine free float is smaller than the market value suggests.

moderator_conclusion:
Take a starter position here rather than wait for CHF 8.00. That reverses our 31 August conclusion, and it reverses on our own arithmetic rather than on any news.

The business case is unchanged and remains well-evidenced. Six operational commitments made in March 2026 were kept or beaten by August: the full CHF 100 million of merger savings delivered six months early, North America returned to growth after a 12.6% contraction, integration costs guided below the original estimate, and - the one that speaks loudest about management quality - the gap between the adjusted and statutory profit measures narrowed from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million exactly as promised. Growth of 11.6% at a 24.9% adjusted margin, with every region and every line contributing, is a real recovery in a business that was drifting two years ago. Inside it sits a distribution arm growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin that the market values at the group multiple and probably should not.

What changed is the cash number, and it changed twice. The screen surfaced this name at 7.3 times free cash flow with an 11% yield and roughly CHF 350 million of net cash. The net cash was never there - the company reported CHF 408 million of net debt at 30 June 2026, CHF 483 million on a strict recomputation - and that correction stands. But our correction of the cash flow itself, to CHF 117 million on a 29% conversion rate, was wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual statement row and manufactured a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, from chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 - a 69% conversion of reported EBITDA, above its own 60% target - and CHF 174.2 million even on the strict statement basis.

That is decisive because the 29% conversion rate was the load-bearing leg of our own 26% haircut. We wrote that the peer multiples 'attach to businesses converting at 60-70%'. The company converts at 69%, inside that range. The other two haircut legs survive untouched - the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed, and consensus 2026-27 EBITDA of CHF 268-289 million sits well below the CHF 400 million the parts arithmetic capitalises - so the fair value is re-derived conservatively, on our own two published cross-checks with only the cash input replaced: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.09, and a 7.5% yield on CHF 211.7 million gives CHF 12.99 on 217.2 million weighted-average shares. The midpoint is CHF 12.05. The EBITDA anchor stays deliberately unrestored.

The adverse case moves for the same kind of reason. CHF 6.80 was our own parts figure of CHF 7.85 cut a further 13% on an Altman Z-score of 0.7 and negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion. Both numbers are arithmetically right and neither is a solvency signal for this balance sheet: the negative working capital is CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through payables, and leverage was reported at 1.1 times on the same call. The adverse case is the parts figure itself, CHF 7.85.

So the shape of the trade is not the one we described a week ago. Fair value is about 30% above CHF 9.25 and the adverse case about 15% below it - roughly two to one, against the balanced payoff we published and declined. Every reservation that made us wait is still live and none of it is priced away: growth decelerates in the second half on management's own four-percentage-point admission, Microsoft cuts partner margin from October 2026 on the largest profit line, capital spending doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 and will take free cash flow from CHF 211.7 million toward CHF 145-160 million while it runs, the stock sits 21% above its 200-day average after gapping 9.5% on results ten days ago, and some CHF 311 million of near-dated floating-rate borrowings refinances into a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September. That is why this is a starter rather than a full seat, and why conviction goes to four and not higher: the catalyst has already fired, no dated event ahead forces the re-rating, and the terminal question about a labour business in an artificial-intelligence deflation remains open.

What would take it higher: full-year 2026 free cash flow holding above CHF 200 million through the capital-spending step-up, or the October Microsoft change passing without a visible mark on direct-business growth. What would take it off: second-half growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, or 2026 free cash flow below CHF 175 million. And it remains a better trade below CHF 8.00, where the entry price meets the adverse case; we are simply no longer willing to insist on that level for a two-to-one payoff.

One caveat on verification, now largely closed. Our licensed feed returns no news and no press releases for this symbol between 1 August and 7 September 2026, and the only dated corporate event in that window - the executive board reorganisation effective 1 September - was pre-announced on the 26 August call. The drift from CHF 9.71 to CHF 9.25 was a thin tape, not an announcement.

sop_breakdown:
Base case, reconciling the favourable and adverse parts and then anchoring on cash rather than on adjusted profit. The parts, on about CHF 400 million of 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA (the level the company's 23-25% margin guidance implies on roughly CHF 1.68 billion of revenue), with the revenue split inferred from the disclosed first-half business-line margins because no segment table was supplied:
- Software and Cloud Direct, about CHF 285 million of EBITDA at 8 times: CHF 2,280 million. The largest profit contributor, growing only 1.5%, with its margin set by Microsoft's incentive policy - hence a discount to Bechtle's live 10.4 times.
- Channel, about CHF 135 million at 12 times: CHF 1,620 million. Growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud since February 2026, and the one part that deserves a premium to the group.
- Services, about CHF 75 million at 10 times: CHF 750 million. Margin repairing from 3.3% to 8.5%, but it is a labour business exposed to bill-rate deflation from artificial intelligence.
- Central and unallocated costs, about minus CHF 95 million capitalised at 9 times: minus CHF 855 million.
- Enterprise value from the parts: about CHF 3,795 million. Less net debt of CHF 450 million (the midpoint of the CHF 408 million the company reports at 30 June 2026 and the CHF 483 million recomputed from the balance sheet) gives equity of CHF 3,345 million, or about CHF 15.60 per share on 215 million shares.

We haircut that by roughly 26%, to CHF 11.50, for three stated reasons: the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed; the parts multiples attach to peers with positive tangible equity, where this balance sheet carries about minus CHF 0.9 billion of tangible book value, CHF 866 million of borrowings and an Altman Z-score of 0.7; and, decisively, adjusted EBITDA here converts to shareholder cash at about 29% (trailing free cash flow of roughly CHF 117 million) against the 60-70% the peer multiples assume, with capital spending set to double to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28.

Two independent cross-checks land in the same place: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.10, and a 7.5% yield on normalised free cash flow of roughly CHF 180 million gives CHF 11.60. CHF 11.50 implies about 7.4 times 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA - still a persistent discount to every peer, deliberately kept for the leverage and the single-vendor dependence.
risk_reward:
From CHF 8.60 today (2026-09-29 quote, vs CHF 9.25 at the 2026-09-22 anchor), the adverse case sits at CHF 7.85 and the base-case fair value at CHF 12.02, with the favourable case at CHF 14.50. That is now about 40% of upside against roughly 9% of downside over an eighteen-month horizon - a payoff of about 4.6 to 1, wider than the two-to-one this record has been carrying, purely because the shares drifted lower (on a thin 70,149-share print, versus a roughly 526,000-share average, with no identifiable company news) while the fair-value and adverse-case levels are unchanged. There is no structural floor beneath the equity - no net cash, no deal terms, no tender offer - so the adverse case is a valuation level rather than a backstop, and it already assumes an orderly de-rating rather than a disorderly one. The discount to fair value is now wider than it was at the anchor, not because the case improved but because the entry got cheaper; the underlying reservations (Microsoft's October 2026 margin cut, second-half growth deceleration, the 2027-28 capital-spending step-up, the near-dated floating-rate refinancing) are all still live and none of them is priced away.

peer_comps_note:
Peer multiples here were pulled live today rather than recalled, because reseller multiples move. On trailing twelve-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA the cohort reads: ALSO Holding 9.0 times, Bechtle 10.4 times, Insight Enterprises 13.1 times, CDW 13.7 times, with Computacenter at 15.1 times enterprise value to free cash flow (its EBITDA multiple is distorted). On earnings the group sits at roughly 18 times (Bechtle, CDW), 19 times (ALSO) and 23 times (Insight). SoftwareOne trades at about 6.2 times its 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA and under 11 times consensus 2027 earnings. The discount is real and it is large.

Three qualifications keep us from spending it all. First, SoftwareOne is not economically identical to the box-movers: its 25% adjusted margin on a much smaller revenue base reflects a licensing-and-services mix closer to Computacenter's than to ALSO's, which argues the right anchor is the middle of the cohort, not the bottom. Second, a meaningful part of the gap is credit-risk-justified rather than mispricing - tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion, the Altman Z-score is 0.7, and net debt is CHF 408-483 million, where Computacenter runs net cash and Bechtle just 1.2 times leverage. Third, and unlike a sector-wide de-rating, this gap is idiosyncratic: the peer cohort has not de-rated together, so the discount is name-specific and does carry genuine potential edge rather than shared sector beta. Closing even half the distance to Bechtle's 10.4 times is worth roughly CHF 4 a share, which is why the question is the durability of cash conversion, not whether the gap exists.

bull_thesis:
SoftwareOne is a repaired business that the market is still pricing as a broken one, and the repair is now documented rather than promised. The company buys software licences and cloud capacity from vendors - overwhelmingly Microsoft, but also Amazon Web Services, Google and Adobe - and resells them to about 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers with advice and managed services wrapped around the transaction. In July 2025 it merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor with a large distribution arm, roughly doubling its size.

The first-half 2026 results, reported on 26 August 2026, are the evidence. Revenue grew 11.6% year on year on a like-for-like basis (comparing the merged company against what the two businesses did separately a year earlier), up from just 1.4% for full-year 2025. Adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, stated before one-off integration costs - reached 24.9% of revenue, a 4.5 percentage-point improvement in a year, with the second quarter alone at 28.9%. Every region grew and every business line grew, including North America, which had shrunk 12.6% in 2025. The entire cost-savings programme was delivered at the top of its CHF 80-100 million range six months early, at CHF 100 million of run-rate savings, and integration costs are now guided lower than first estimated, at CHF 75-85 million rather than CHF 80-100 million. Chief executive Raphael Erb described integration as 'substantially completed'.

Management also did the unglamorous thing it promised in March 2026: it narrowed the gap between its adjusted profit measure and its statutory one, from CHF 33 million of adjustments to CHF 18.4 million. That matters more than the headline margin, because the standing objection to this company was always that the adjusted number flattered a business that earned nothing on a reported basis. A reported EBITDA margin of 22.7% in the first half, up 5.2 percentage points, is now within touching distance of the adjusted figure.

Underneath the recovery sits a genuinely good business the market values at nothing in particular. The channel arm - selling through other resellers rather than direct to end customers - grew 35.6% in the first half at a 57.2% adjusted margin, and in February 2026 became, on the company's own account, the first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud, rolling out across ten markets with more to follow. That is a scalable, vendor-diversifying franchise growing three times as fast as the group, and management has just given its head a seat on the executive board. The services business is repairing in parallel, with its adjusted margin rising from 3.3% to 8.5% in a year on 17.4% growth, led by cloud migration, data and cybersecurity work.

On valuation the arithmetic is stark. At CHF 9.25 the equity is worth about CHF 1.99 billion; adding CHF 408 million of net debt gives an enterprise value near CHF 2.4 billion, or roughly 6.2 times the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA that the company's own 23-25% full-year margin guidance implies on about CHF 1.68 billion of 2026 revenue. Live peer multiples today are 9.0 times at ALSO Holding, 10.4 times at Bechtle, 13.1 times at Insight Enterprises and 13.7 times at CDW. On earnings the gap is just as wide: consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 puts the stock on under 11 times, against 18-23 times for the same peer group. Every single turn of enterprise-value-to-EBITDA re-rating is worth about CHF 1.85 a share.

The conditions this case depends on are specific and checkable. Microsoft's 5% margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint, effective October 2026, must prove as immaterial as Erb asserts. Second-half 2026 growth must decelerate only modestly from the four-percentage-point pull-forward tailwind management has already flagged. The 2027-28 step-up in capital spending to about 8% of revenue must genuinely be funded from released working capital rather than from shareholders. And cash conversion, which the chief financial officer put at 69% on the 26 August call - free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 against CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA, above the company's own 60% target and inside the 60-70% band the peer multiples assume - must hold there through the capital-spending step-up rather than sagging back. If those hold, a business earning CHF 0.85-1.00 per share by 2027-28 with a scaling distribution arm should not trade at ten times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The cheapness that put this stock on the screen was overstated by the screen and then understated by our own first correction of it. On the company's own figures the discount is real, so the bear case has to rest on what the next two years do to that cash rather than on a claim that it was never there.

Start with the number our file got wrong twice over. The screen carried CHF 585 million of trailing free cash flow and a 7.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, which is nonsense. But our first correction of it - to roughly CHF 117 million, a 5.9% yield and a 29% conversion rate - was also wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual cash-flow row and invented a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, given by chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August 2026 call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 - operating cash flow of CHF 271.6 million less CHF 71.9 million of capital spending - a 69% conversion of the CHF 308 million of reported EBITDA and above the company's own above-60% target. On the strict statement basis it is CHF 174.2 million. What survives from the original objection is narrower but still real: the screen's own figure is unusable because this balance sheet carries CHF 4.5 billion of receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of payables, so any single date's cash figure is a snapshot of supplier-payment timing, and full-year reseller cash flow captures the year-end float peak. The bear case is therefore about the durability of that 69%, not its existence.

Second, there is no net cash. Our prior note credited roughly CHF 350 million of it. The company reported net debt of CHF 408 million at 30 June 2026, up from CHF 369.3 million at the end of 2025; recomputed strictly from the balance sheet the figure is CHF 483 million. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million - a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolving credit facility - against CHF 383 million of cash, and roughly 36% of those borrowings, some CHF 311 million, fall due inside twelve months, more than the revolver draw alone. Behind the debt there is no book cushion: goodwill and acquired intangibles of CHF 1.89 billion exceed shareholders' equity of CHF 0.99 billion, so tangible book value is about minus CHF 0.9 billion. That is a statement about recovery in a liquidation, not a solvency signal - Schraner put leverage at 1.1 times on the same call, and the negative net working capital of minus CHF 509 million is the reseller model itself rather than distress. The bear objection here is price, not survival: in a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September, a mid-cap rolling CHF 311 million of near-dated, largely floating-rate borrowings on a net financial charge already running about CHF 52 million a year pays more for them than it did.

Third, the growth just reported is partly borrowed from the future. Erb conceded on the August call that early customer renewals ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase contributed 'around 4 percentage points' of the 11.6% first-half growth, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Strip the pull-forward and underlying growth is closer to 7-8%. The direct business - still the largest profit contributor - grew only 1.5% in the half and actually declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Fourth, the profit pool is set by a supplier, not by the company. Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management's answer - 'there is absolutely no material impact for us' - is an assertion with a hope attached, that reductions 'should largely be balanced by other incentive opportunity'. This is the same vendor whose previous incentive change produced a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America, and management sounded similarly relaxed going into that one.

Fifth, the cash-generation story gets worse precisely when the market expects it to get better. Capital spending rises to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28, roughly double the current run rate, to fund the automation that underwrites the 2030 margin ambition. The chief financial officer says the funding 'will come from the release of net working capital. So it should be in a way cash neutral.' Working capital can be released once; the spending recurs. On roughly CHF 1.8 billion of revenue that is CHF 130-145 million a year of capital spending against about CHF 75 million today - some CHF 60-70 million a year off free cash flow, which would take the CHF 211.7 million just reported down toward CHF 145-160 million through the investment years even if operating margins do everything management promises. The 69% conversion rate is a starting point, not a run rate.

Sixth, the statutory record remains poor and the multiple already reflects a recovery. Net income was CHF 21 million in 2023, minus CHF 2 million in 2024 and CHF 0.9 million in 2025; earnings per share have compounded at minus 70% a year over five years. The company has beaten earnings expectations in 2 of the last 7 quarters. And the market is no longer ignoring the turn: the stock gapped 9.5% higher on the results (CHF 8.65 to CHF 9.47 on 26 August 2026, on four times normal volume), sits 21% above its 200-day average and 92% of the way up its 52-week range after rising from a low of CHF 5.83.

Finally, the terminal question. Roughly half of revenue is a services business earning 8.5% - the economics of billing people's time at a spread, which is exactly the model artificial intelligence deflates. Management's own 2030 margin bridge is built on 'AI and automation efficiencies', which is another way of saying the work will need fewer people. A company can win that efficiency race internally and still lose the bill rates that came with selling the hours. Add hyperscalers and software vendors selling ever more directly through their own marketplaces, and the intermediary's long-run reason to exist is a live question rather than a settled one. What confirms this case: second-half 2026 growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, free cash flow for 2026 below CHF 175 million against the CHF 211.7 million just reported, or any commentary walking back the October Microsoft change as immaterial.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the recovery - the market saw that on 26 August and paid 9.5% for it - but about what the recovered business converts into cash.

The visible street position is internally inconsistent, and the inconsistency is instructive. The eleven analysts modelling revenue put 2027 at about CHF 1.74 billion; the ten modelling earnings put 2027 earnings per share at CHF 0.85 and 2028 at CHF 0.94. But the handful modelling EBITDA carry CHF 289 million for 2027 - a 16.6% margin, against a company guiding 23-25% and delivering 24.9% in the first half of 2026. Either those EBITDA estimates are stale pre-merger assumptions, or the analysts are quietly refusing to capitalise the adjusted measure. We think it is partly both, and that the refusal is more right than wrong.

Our own view sits between the two. The adjusted profitability is real as an operating result - the narrowing of adjustments from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million is the proof - but it converts to shareholder cash at well under half: after roughly CHF 41 million of interest, a guided 30% tax rate, and capital spending that management has told us doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28. Trailing free cash flow of about CHF 117 million is 29% of the CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA the guidance implies. The peer multiples we are being invited to close the gap to attach to businesses converting at 60-70%. So the honest anchor is 12-13 times earnings, not 9-10 times EBITDA - which is exactly why we arrive at CHF 11.50 and not the CHF 15-plus the raw parts arithmetic produces.

Where the street is genuinely too bearish is the channel business. Nobody is valuing a line growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, newly authorised as Google Cloud's first global distributor and rolling out country by country, at anything other than the group multiple. Management just put its head on the executive board, which is where a company signals what it thinks it is becoming. That is the piece of this sum-of-the-parts the market is not pricing separately, and it is the reason a discount this wide should not persist indefinitely.

The specific street assumption we think is wrong in the other direction is the treatment of Microsoft's October 2026 margin reduction as a non-event because management called it 'absolutely no material impact'. The company said something similar before the last incentive change, which cost it a full year of declining direct revenue and a 12.6% contraction in North America.
forcing_function:
There is no dated event that forces a re-rating, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. The re-rating trigger that existed - the delivery of the merger savings - fired on 26 August 2026 and the market paid for it the same day.

What remains is a sequence of scheduled proof points, each of which either extends or breaks the recovery narrative:
- Full-year 2026 results, due around the end of the first quarter of 2027 (the 2025 full year was reported on 31 March 2026). This is the one that matters. Three numbers decide it: where the full-year adjusted margin lands inside the 23-25% guide, whether the direct business returned to growth in the second half as management promised, and what free cash flow actually printed for the year against the CHF 117 million trailing figure.
- October 2026, when Microsoft's 5% partner-margin reduction on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint takes effect. This is a dated risk event rather than a catalyst, and management has staked credibility on it being immaterial. It is now two days away.
- The 2027-28 capital-spending programme, which will show up in cash-flow statements from the 2027 half-year onward and will settle the argument about whether adjusted profitability reaches shareholders.
- A residual and unhandicapped possibility: a business generating CHF 400 million of adjusted EBITDA with an integration completed, a scaling distribution arm and a market value under CHF 2 billion is the kind of asset that attracts strategic or private-equity attention. That was the story in 2023-24 and it failed. We do not underwrite it and it carries no weight in the conviction here.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where this thesis is most exposed, and the risks are dated rather than speculative.

The growth comparison turns immediately. Management disclosed on 26 August that roughly four percentage points of the 11.6% first-half growth came from customers renewing early ahead of Microsoft's July 2026 price increase, and that the second half decelerates as a result. Underlying growth is therefore nearer 7-8%, and the reported second-half number will look materially weaker than the first-half one for reasons that are arithmetic rather than operational. Investors who bought the 26 August print will be marking a slowdown.

Microsoft cuts partner margin by 5% on Microsoft 365 E1 and E3, OneDrive and SharePoint from October 2026. Management expects no material impact. If that proves optimistic it lands directly on the direct business, which is the largest profit contributor and which already grew only 1.5% in the first half and declined 1.8% in the second quarter.

Cash is the pinch point rather than profit. Free cash flow was CHF 28.1 million in the first half of 2026 and roughly CHF 117 million over twelve months. Capital spending steps up to about 8% of revenue across 2027-28 - some CHF 130-145 million a year against roughly CHF 75 million today - funded, the chief financial officer says, 'from the release of net working capital'. Releasing working capital in a business whose current assets are CHF 4.5 billion of receivables means collecting faster or paying suppliers slower, and it can only be done once. There is no cash-burn hump in the equity-risk sense - the company is profitable - but there is a real risk that 2027 free cash flow prints near CHF 110-125 million and the market concludes the margin story never reaches the shareholder.

The balance sheet compounds this. Gross borrowings are CHF 866 million (a CHF 550 million term loan plus CHF 200 million drawn on the revolver) against CHF 383 million of cash, with an interest bill running about CHF 41 million a year on largely floating-rate facilities. The current market regime is a tightening one - the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 58-60% to raise rates on 15-16 September 2026 after payrolls of 162,000 erased the prior soft print - with an oil shock running alongside it (Brent up 9.3% to about USD 96 over the 29-30 August weekend) and equity volatility printing below 14, which is complacency rather than comfort. A levered mid-cap with negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion and an Altman Z-score of 0.7 is not where you want to be holding when a complacent tape reprices. There is no near-term maturity wall we can identify from the materials - the bridge facility was repaid in January 2026 - but refinancing the term loan happens at higher rates than it was struck at.

One structural comfort worth naming: none of these risks are the market's shared risk. This thesis resolves on Microsoft's incentive policy and on the company's own cash conversion, not on oil, not on artificial-intelligence capital spending, and not on the rate path except through the interest bill. In a book where too many positions resolve on the same macro driver, that independence has value.

positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling in this name has largely already happened, which is a point in the stock's favour rather than against it.

Two forced-seller cohorts were created by the July 2025 Crayon merger. First, share count rose from about 152 million to about 217 million - roughly 65 million new shares issued to Crayon's holders, many of them Norwegian institutions and index funds that owned a Norwegian small-cap for Norwegian reasons and inherited a Swiss mid-cap. Any merger lock-up has long since lapsed, more than thirteen months on, and the drift of the shares through the first half of 2026 to a low of CHF 5.83 is consistent with that supply being worked off.

Second, the income buyers. The dividend has been roughly halved per share while the share count rose 43%: the company paid CHF 32.4 million in the first half of 2026 on about 215 million shares, some 15 centimes a share, against CHF 45.6 million in the first half of 2025 on about 152 million shares, some 30 centimes. For a Swiss mid-cap, income holders are a meaningful part of the register, and a halved per-share payout is exactly the trigger that forces a yield mandate to sell irrespective of value. That repricing sits behind the stock rather than in front of it.

What could still force selling is passive rather than active: a levered Swiss mid-cap that has run 59% off its low is a candidate for momentum and quality-factor flows in both directions, and average daily volume of about 526,000 shares against a CHF 2 billion market value means the register turns slowly. Today's print of CHF 9.25 came on roughly 125,000 shares, a quarter of normal - a thin tape, not conviction selling. The founder and anchor shareholders remain a large stable block, which cuts both ways: it dampens forced selling and it also means genuine free float is smaller than the market value suggests.

moderator_conclusion:
Take a starter position here rather than wait for CHF 8.00. That reverses our 31 August conclusion, and it reverses on our own arithmetic rather than on any news.

The business case is unchanged and remains well-evidenced. Six operational commitments made in March 2026 were kept or beaten by August: the full CHF 100 million of merger savings delivered six months early, North America returned to growth after a 12.6% contraction, integration costs guided below the original estimate, and - the one that speaks loudest about management quality - the gap between the adjusted and statutory profit measures narrowed from CHF 33 million to CHF 18.4 million exactly as promised. Growth of 11.6% at a 24.9% adjusted margin, with every region and every line contributing, is a real recovery in a business that was drifting two years ago. Inside it sits a distribution arm growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin that the market values at the group multiple and probably should not.

What changed is the cash number, and it changed twice. The screen surfaced this name at 7.3 times free cash flow with an 11% yield and roughly CHF 350 million of net cash. The net cash was never there - the company reported CHF 408 million of net debt at 30 June 2026, CHF 483 million on a strict recomputation - and that correction stands. But our correction of the cash flow itself, to CHF 117 million on a 29% conversion rate, was wrong: it double-counted a semi-annual statement row and manufactured a phantom second half of 2025. The company's own figure, from chief financial officer Hanspeter Schraner on the 26 August call, is free cash flow of CHF 211.7 million for the twelve months to June 2026 - a 69% conversion of reported EBITDA, above its own 60% target - and CHF 174.2 million even on the strict statement basis.

That is decisive because the 29% conversion rate was the load-bearing leg of our own 26% haircut. We wrote that the peer multiples 'attach to businesses converting at 60-70%'. The company converts at 69%, inside that range. The other two haircut legs survive untouched - the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed, and consensus 2026-27 EBITDA of CHF 268-289 million sits well below the CHF 400 million the parts arithmetic capitalises - so the fair value is re-derived conservatively, on our own two published cross-checks with only the cash input replaced: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.09, and a 7.5% yield on CHF 211.7 million gives CHF 12.99 on 217.2 million weighted-average shares. The midpoint is CHF 12.05. The EBITDA anchor stays deliberately unrestored.

The adverse case moves for the same kind of reason. CHF 6.80 was our own parts figure of CHF 7.85 cut a further 13% on an Altman Z-score of 0.7 and negative tangible book value of about minus CHF 0.9 billion. Both numbers are arithmetically right and neither is a solvency signal for this balance sheet: the negative working capital is CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through receivables against CHF 4.5 billion of pass-through payables, and leverage was reported at 1.1 times on the same call. The adverse case is the parts figure itself, CHF 7.85.

So the shape of the trade is not the one we described a week ago. Fair value is about 30% above CHF 9.25 and the adverse case about 15% below it - roughly two to one, against the balanced payoff we published and declined. Every reservation that made us wait is still live and none of it is priced away: growth decelerates in the second half on management's own four-percentage-point admission, Microsoft cuts partner margin from October 2026 on the largest profit line, capital spending doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 and will take free cash flow from CHF 211.7 million toward CHF 145-160 million while it runs, the stock sits 21% above its 200-day average after gapping 9.5% on results ten days ago, and some CHF 311 million of near-dated floating-rate borrowings refinances into a tape where the Federal Reserve is priced roughly 60% to raise rates in mid-September. That is why this is a starter rather than a full seat, and why conviction goes to four and not higher: the catalyst has already fired, no dated event ahead forces the re-rating, and the terminal question about a labour business in an artificial-intelligence deflation remains open.

What would take it higher: full-year 2026 free cash flow holding above CHF 200 million through the capital-spending step-up, or the October Microsoft change passing without a visible mark on direct-business growth. What would take it off: second-half growth below about 6%, a full-year adjusted margin at the low end of the 23-25% guide, or 2026 free cash flow below CHF 175 million. And it remains a better trade below CHF 8.00, where the entry price meets the adverse case; we are simply no longer willing to insist on that level for a two-to-one payoff.

One caveat on verification, now largely closed. Our licensed feed returns no news and no press releases for this symbol between 1 August and 7 September 2026, and the only dated corporate event in that window - the executive board reorganisation effective 1 September - was pre-announced on the 26 August call. The drift from CHF 9.71 to CHF 9.25 was a thin tape, not an announcement.

sop_breakdown:
Base case, reconciling the favourable and adverse parts and then anchoring on cash rather than on adjusted profit. The parts, on about CHF 400 million of 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA (the level the company's 23-25% margin guidance implies on roughly CHF 1.68 billion of revenue), with the revenue split inferred from the disclosed first-half business-line margins because no segment table was supplied:
- Software and Cloud Direct, about CHF 285 million of EBITDA at 8 times: CHF 2,280 million. The largest profit contributor, growing only 1.5%, with its margin set by Microsoft's incentive policy - hence a discount to Bechtle's live 10.4 times.
- Channel, about CHF 135 million at 12 times: CHF 1,620 million. Growing 35.6% at a 57.2% margin, first global authorised distributor for Google Cloud since February 2026, and the one part that deserves a premium to the group.
- Services, about CHF 75 million at 10 times: CHF 750 million. Margin repairing from 3.3% to 8.5%, but it is a labour business exposed to bill-rate deflation from artificial intelligence.
- Central and unallocated costs, about minus CHF 95 million capitalised at 9 times: minus CHF 855 million.
- Enterprise value from the parts: about CHF 3,795 million. Less net debt of CHF 450 million (the midpoint of the CHF 408 million the company reports at 30 June 2026 and the CHF 483 million recomputed from the balance sheet) gives equity of CHF 3,345 million, or about CHF 15.60 per share on 215 million shares.

We haircut that by roughly 26%, to CHF 11.50, for three stated reasons: the segment split is inferred rather than disclosed; the parts multiples attach to peers with positive tangible equity, where this balance sheet carries about minus CHF 0.9 billion of tangible book value, CHF 866 million of borrowings and an Altman Z-score of 0.7; and, decisively, adjusted EBITDA here converts to shareholder cash at about 29% (trailing free cash flow of roughly CHF 117 million) against the 60-70% the peer multiples assume, with capital spending set to double to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28.

Two independent cross-checks land in the same place: 13 times consensus 2027 earnings per share of CHF 0.85 gives CHF 11.10, and a 7.5% yield on normalised free cash flow of roughly CHF 180 million gives CHF 11.60. CHF 11.50 implies about 7.4 times 2026 estimated adjusted EBITDA - still a persistent discount to every peer, deliberately kept for the leverage and the single-vendor dependence.
